 White House fires cybersecurity chief after widespread outages 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP)—Cyber security chief Sean Cairncross was fired from his post, a source close to the White House told AFP on Thursday, following major outages and growing concerns about AI threats.

US President Donald Trump fully supported the firing because Cairncross lacked proper credentials to perform the job, the source said.

His role will be filled in an acting capacity by current Defense Department Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies, who has more appropriate credentials and has been Senate-confirmed, the source said.

In recent days and weeks, major outages in America have disrupted travel, communications and e-commerce for countless users, but also affected a top-secret internal communications network at the National Security Administration.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio congratulated Davies on X, writing: “Congratulations to the new National Cyber Director Kirsten Davies — look forward to working together to strengthen America’s cybersecurity.”

Prior to serving as National Cyber Director, Cairncross filled various roles as a White House insider during Trump’s first term.

Prior to that, Cairncross worked as the Republican National Committee’s Chief Operating Officer for the 2016 election cycle.

 Putin vows ‘more painful’ response to Ukraine for Crimea bridge attack 







SHENZHEN, China (AFP)—Russia’s Vladimir Putin vowed Thursday that Moscow will respond to Ukraine’s attack on the Crimea bridge with “much more painful” strikes.

Putin spoke in China after meeting with Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. Ukraine had two days earlier struck the 19-kilometre (12-mile) bridge — a symbol of Putin’s rule — severing the part of it used by vehicles.

“We will respond to these attacks. Our response will be far more painful than Kyiv’s attack on the bridge,” Putin said.

“We will, of course, rebuild the bridge,” he added.

Images published by Ukraine’s SBU security service appeared to show a long section of the road in rubble in the sea, and one of two symbolic white arches collapsed after the attack.

Ukraine has hit it three times in a week, with another strike on Thursday temporarily halting train services. It was unclear how much further damage was sustained, and officials said trains had resumed transiting over the bridge in the afternoon.

Putin opened the bridge personally in 2018, four years after his government annexed Crimea from Ukraine.

“The plan to rebuild it has been agreed,” Russian Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin, said Thursday, saying it should be approved in the coming days before work can start.

Ukraine has targeted the bridge several times during the war.

Moscow seized Crimea from Ukraine in 2014 after a pro-EU revolution overthrew a Kremlin-backed government in Kyiv. Fighting between Russian-backed rebels and Kyiv ensued afterwards.

news.text:
"I would like to congratulate the leaders of Russia, China, and the United States for proceeding to have such an important meeting in Shenzhen. Billions of people on our relatively small planet hope that these three large powers can begin to chart a path forward that leads to peace and stability for the world as a whole, and an end to the idea of unilateral hegemonism," Sare said, commenting on the meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump.

"President Trump once commented that if the United States and China worked together, there is no problem that couldn’t be solved. If the United States, Russia, and China cooperate to diminish the threat of war, and to uphold universal principles of human dignity and justice, no one will be able to stop the progress of mankind," the US presidential candidate emphasized.

At the same time, she pointed out that "there are some, particularly in the UK and EU, who are unhappy that this meeting occurred". "I think we would be justified in questioning their motives. How can one object to diplomacy?" Sare noted.

"I don’t expect that these preliminary talks will bring an immediate end to the unjustified war against Iran, the crimes Israel is committing against her neighbors, or a resolution to the Ukraine conflict, but I believe that an important step has finally been taken in the right direction, and I am hopeful that more steps will follow in the same path," she emphasized.

The presidents of Russia, the United States and China held a meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, the first such meeting ever. The heads of state exchanged views on the current international situation and expressed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security. The leaders also adopted a declaration on peace.

news.title: Pro-life group says Trump admin didn't give key abortion drug commitments before Overton FDA nomination pulled
news.text: A leading pro-life group said it opposed advancing Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration without commitments from the Trump administration on abortion drug policy. The White House withdrew her nomination this week amid questions about her support in the Senate. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Erik Baptist, senior vice president of legal strategy at Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, said his group asked the Senate to hold up Overton’s confirmation until it received "firm commitments" from the administration on two fronts regarding abortion drug policy. Baptist said the group wants the next FDA nominee to commit to ending mail-order access to abortion drugs authorized under the Biden administration and changing how the agency studies the safety of those pills. "Right now, we’re seeing more abortions in this country than before the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade," Baptist said. "That’s precisely because of what the Biden FDA did to authorize mail-order abortion drugs. We’re seeing upwards of 15,000 abortion drugs and abortions occurring in pro-life states. Those states can’t meaningfully enforce their laws while this nationwide policy is in place." WHITE HOUSE PULLS TRUMP'S FDA PICK HEIDI OVERTON ON EVE OF SENATE PANEL VOTE "Under the Biden-era policy, anybody can obtain these drugs online and receive them through the mail," he continued. "When I say anybody, we’ve seen news story after news story every week about men and other predators obtaining these drugs to coerce or poison women into taking them against their will. Until that policy changes, no pregnant woman is safe from these drugs. My question to this administration is: How many more women have to be poisoned or coerced with abortion drugs before you take action on this drug?" Under the Biden administration, the FDA eliminated the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone, allowing it to be prescribed without an in-person visit by certified prescribers and dispensed by certified pharmacies through the mail. On the group's second point of concern, Baptist said the FDA needs to conduct a new study to show the safety — or lack thereof — of mifepristone. "The problem is that the study is significantly flawed," he said. "It’s almost designed to fail and not lead to future changes to the drug regimen. We have asked for more robust data because significant information is currently lacking, including transparency into the agency’s methodology and an invitation for outside experts who have studied this drug over the last few decades." "This is something that should be bipartisan. Everybody should support better data, more transparency and outside experts who can inform an agency that has never conducted such a study before," he added. Several pro-life groups and Republican lawmakers have urged the Trump administration to complete the FDA’s safety review of mifepristone and consider reinstating safeguards, while some have called for removing the drug from the market. The FDA said the review is ongoing, with study results expected in December 2026 and a final report expected by March 2027. The White House pulled Overton’s nomination to lead the FDA earlier this week, one day before a Senate committee vote. President Donald Trump picked Overton, a physician and White House advisor, in August to succeed Marty Makary, who resigned from the position in May. Kyle Diamantas has led the agency in an acting capacity since Makary’s departure. WOMAN WHO SAYS ABORTION PILLS NEARLY KILLED HER URGES RFK JR TO ACT AS GROUP DEMANDS MAIL-ORDER CRACKDOWN Overton also previously served as vice chair and chief policy officer at the America First Policy Institute, a conservative think tank, where she criticized expanded access to abortion pills in a 2023 policy brief. The White House said Overton lacked the votes on Capitol Hill and pulled her nomination, although Sen. Bill Cassidy, chair of the Senate health committee, contended that he believed she could have been confirmed. "The White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH said that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members," Cassidy, R-La., wrote on X. "I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate." Baptist said he did not know whether the White House was concerned about pro-life votes or other constituencies but thinks Cassidy "was making progress with the administration to secure the commitments we were seeking and asking the Senate to hold the administration accountable for." Cassidy had criticized Overton for supporting Trump’s decision to recommend changes to the childhood vaccine schedule, but the senator said he had been convinced she was right for the job after she committed to "follow the science." She had appeared alongside Trump in the Oval Office as the president signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations, including a recommendation to administer measles, mumps and rubella vaccines separately once individual shots become available domestically. Cassidy said at a September hearing that there was no scientific evidence for Trump’s suggestion that the combined shot could be "quite lethal" and warned the remark could discourage vaccination. "Yes, senator, the MMR vaccine is safe and effective," Overton told Cassidy. Pressed on what she would do if Trump asked her to disregard the FDA’s safety standards, Overton said she would give the president her best advice and follow the legal requirements for reviewing individual products. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., asked Overton directly whether Trump was wrong. Overton reiterated that the vaccine was safe and effective and called it the best tool available during the measles outbreak. Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., questioned why she had not corrected Trump in the Oval Office. "Why should we expect you to stand up to the president as FDA commissioner?" Markey asked. Baptist said he wants the next FDA commissioner to be somebody who "understands science" and has experience managing an agency. "The FDA is a very large bureaucracy with multiple constituencies, so understanding how science is conducted and how drugs are approved will be essential to any successful candidate or nominee for the position," he said. But, Baptist said, the administration does not have to wait for an FDA nominee to take the position before it can take the action on abortion pill policy that his group desires. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The good news is that it doesn’t have to be the nominee who makes these commitments. The administration can do it because it has admitted that it can take these actions immediately using its own authority," he argued. "That power is within the administration’s possession. It’s a matter of political will, not legal ability." "With regard to fixing the study, I think they can make those changes now," Baptist continued. "They don’t need to wait for a confirmation, especially when they’re saying they’re going to finish the study in December of this year. We might not have an FDA commissioner at that point, or even a nominee. So they need to fix it immediately and course-correct the study before it’s fatally flawed and completed next year." Fox News' Stepheny Price contributed to this report.
news.summary: Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America opposed Heidi Overton's FDA confirmation until the Trump administration committed to ending mail-order abortion drugs.
news.author: Landon Mion

news.title: Rival summit on Ukraine pushes for European role in talks to end war
news.text:
European leaders have expressed their readiness to negotiate with Russia to end the war in Ukraine, insisting that Europe must have a seat at the table. 

Speaking at the Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, British prime minister Andy Burnham said Europe had a “united negotiating position”, while German chancellor Friedrich Merz argued Russia’s “maximalist demands” were unrealistic. 

“The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase,” Mr Merz added. 

US envoy Jared Kushner said Donald Trump wanted to reach a deal with Europe’s support, adding the president believed “peace is achievable” following his meeting with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Chinese president Xi Jinping at the Apec summit in Shenzhen.

Mr Kushner and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff travelled to Berlin to brief some 40 European leaders on Mr Trump’s efforts to end the nearly five-year war following his historic trilateral talks with Mr Putin and Mr Xi this week.

Mr Kushner said Russia was open to European participation in peace negotiations and appeared “comfortable” with Ukraine receiving security guarantees enshrined in Nato’s Article Five, which requires allies to defend a member under attack. 

“I think we have gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” he said. “And I think that comes with at least what the Russians are saying, which is that their intention when this war is over is to not have another war in the future.”

“Any deal we do will be in close consultation with Ukraine and with Europe,” he added. “And that’s something that he also asked us to come here today and reassure people in that regard.”

However, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky remained sceptical, saying Mr Putin had repeatedly rejected proposals for peace. “Putin has always said no,” he said. 

Mr Merz said European leaders were willing to hold “serious discussions on European security” with Russia, but only after a “peace agreement with Ukraine” and on terms acceptable to both Kyiv and its allies. 

French president Emmanuel Macron urged allies to do the “maximum” to strengthen Ukraine’s air defences and “reopen the question” of the country’s membership in Nato.

Mr Kushner said Mr Trump used his talks with the leaders of Russia and China to “send a very strong message to both of them on the desire for peace. 

While declining to disclose details of the “private discussions”, Mr Kushner said the US president had emerged from the talks convinced a resolution was possible. 

“I believe he also came away believing that peace is achievable and we need to all work together to try and achieve it,” he said.

Mr Putin said in Shenzhen that Moscow was open to involving European countries in the negotiations, but “we need to understand with what Europe will come to these negotiations”. 

He said the Kremlin had employed diplomatic channels to invite European officials to Moscow “to determine their position”, but did not offer further details. No date had been set for the proposed meeting.

Despite these diplomatic efforts, there are few signs that Moscow is prepared to scale back its military campaign. Russia continues to attack Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as winter approaches and Mr Putin maintains his territorial demands. He also threatened a stronger response to Ukraine’s latest strike on the Crime bridge.
news.summary: US envoys reassure European leaders that Donald Trump’s talks with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen can pave the way for peace
news.author: Maroosha Muzaffar

news.title: Xi Jinping Leans On Trump As China Seeks To Contain Chip War With US
news.text: Xi Jinping showed Donald Trump extraordinary hospitality during their third summit of the year. For Beijing, that bonhomie might be its best strategy for stopping a spiraling chip battle with its main rival.China's top leader broke nearly five decades of precedent to give Trump a rare airport welcome - and cheek-to-cheek hug - as the Republican touched down Wednesday in Shenzhen. Over an afternoon of discussions at a secluded state guesthouse the following day, Trump lauded Xi as a friend, while Xi praised his US counterpart's effort to steady bilateral ties as "one for the history books." In another show of closeness, Trump, 80, was seen offering Xi, 73, a hand as they boarded an escalator, with the Chinese leader holding the Republican's forearm as he stepped up beside him.The camaraderie stood out coming days after Washington stepped up efforts to restrict China's access to the technology underpinning the global AI race. Both leaders appeared to lean heavily on their personal rapport to keep ties between the world's largest economies on an even keel, a departure from the tit-for-tat of last year's trade war.Photo Credit: Bloomberg"Trump is Xi's best option," said Alicia Garcia Herrero, chief Asia-Pacific economist at Natixis SA. Officials in Beijing realize newly exposed divisions within the administration are driving the latest curbs, giving Beijing an incentive to preserve its relationship with the president. "Things could get worse. China needs to stop this spiral of additional export controls. It's very important for China."Xi's team now needs to "negotiate night and day" with the friendly pockets of Trump's team before next month's Group of 20 leaders' summit in Miami, she said, and hold off on reimposing controls on rare earths - a move that would blow up their hard-won trade truce.China's resolve will be tested later this month when its suspension of a ban on exports of critical minerals to the US, including gallium, germanium and antimony, is set to expire. In a sign Beijing is already mulling some retaliation, China's Commerce Ministry earlier this week threatened countermeasures against Washington's latest salvo, if some resolution couldn't be reached.For now, this week's summitry offered evidence that both leaders remain determined to prevent their rivalry from spiraling into a confrontation that would inflict pain on their own economies."You're my friend, and we have a very special relationship," Trump told Xi at the start of their meeting, while flanked by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose agencies helped draft the latest curbs. "I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we'll never have a problem," added the US president, who has two years left in the White House. After the Xi-Trump huddle spilled over into an impromptu lunch that kept Russian President Vladimir Putin waiting for their delayed trilateral, China called the discussions "positive and constructive." Both sides vowed to develop an action plan for building a "constructive relationship of strategic stability," and pledged greater cooperation on artificial intelligence and drug controls, according to the Chinese readout."Any disagreements that cannot be resolved immediately should be managed constructively to prevent conflicts from escalating," Xi said, in a veiled reference to Washington's latest barrage of measures.The US has yet to publish its own account of the talks.Zhu Feng, dean of the School of International Studies at Nanjing University, called the encounter on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum the "friendliest, most positive" meeting between Xi and Trump this year. The aftermath from Nvidia Corp. co-founder Jensen Huang's downfall, however, could still spark a major escalation in the US-China tech war, and change the calculus, he said."It is clear this summit will not alter the fundamental choices the US has made to engage in strategic competition with China," he said. "China-US relations are unlikely to undergo any substantive change as a result of summit-level diplomacy. We need not harbor excessive illusions in this regard."Tech WarThe talks on Thursday were held in Kylin Villa, which opened in 1997, the year neighboring Hong Kong was handed back to Beijing from Britain. That resort has since hosted Chinese leaders and high-profile foreign visitors, and is also personal to Xi being the place where his father - Xi Zhongxun - once recuperated while battling cancer.Its lakeside location contrasts sharply with the rest of futuristic Shenzhen: the beating heart of China's robotics and drone industries and home to Huawei Technologies Co. - the national champion chasing Nvidia to produce cutting-edge AI chips.China's decision to host its summit in that city ensured the tech battle with America was the backdrop to the pleasantries, as the next deadline for extending their trade truce on Jan. 10 looms large.Trump tried to reduce tensions by downplaying allegations Huang had an affair with a Chinese executive who US intelligence believes was spying for China. "Any pretty woman that comes from China, they considered her to be a spy," he said.The US leader also appeared keen to distinguish between restricting China's access to the most sophisticated semiconductors and allowing US companies to continue selling less advanced products.Expectations for major breakthroughs were low going into the summit, especially given both leaders are meeting again next month. But even a commencement date for the reduction on $30 billion worth of each other's imports, negotiated under the newly established US-China Board of Trade, didn't materialize in the initial readouts. A similar framework has been floated for bilateral investment, though progress has been slow. Tensions could soon flare again. US lawmakers in Washington are closing in on a deal to ban Chinese cars from the US, according to people familiar with the matter.For now, both presidents want to reinforce their personal ties ahead of a potentially more confrontational period when the new US Congress takes office in January, said William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group."The Democrats are signaling strongly they are going to look hard into pushing the administration to enforce or reinstate strict export control measures against high-end AI semiconductor chips," he said. "Beijing is sensing there might be a storm coming in the next few weeks."(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: China's top leader broke nearly five decades of precedent to give Trump a rare airport welcome - and cheek-to-cheek hug - as the Republican touched down Wednesday in Shenzhen.

news.title: Can never sit at this table: Rahul Gandhi jabs PM over Trump-Xi-Putin meet
news.text: Congress MP and Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Friday took a swipe at Prime Minister Narendra Modi over his absence from a high-profile meeting of US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China, calling him a "compromised PM".Sharing a photograph of the three leaders sitting together, Rahul suggested that India's Prime Minister would have been part of the gathering had the Congress been in power."If Congress were in power, India's Prime Minister would be sitting at this table," Rahul Gandhi wrote in a post on X. The meeting has drawn attention amid the growing prominence of the term 'G3', used to describe the three leaders and their countries.TRUMP, XI AND PUTIN HOLD TRILATERAL MEETINGThe meeting between the three leaders primarily focused on the ongoing wars and efforts to reduce nuclear arsenals. They also discussed the international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security.The leaders adopted a joint declaration titled 'The Russia-China-US Heads of State Declaration Toward Peace'.According to the declaration, the three countries agreed to work towards reforming the United Nations, increasing the production and supply of refined petroleum products, and holding discussions on reducing nuclear risks.The Russian and US presidents also expressed appreciation to China for hosting the trilateral summit.BJP HITS BACK AT RAHUL GANDHIThe BJP responded to Rahul Gandhi's remarks, accusing the Congress of having compromised India's diplomatic interests and national security during its time in power.In a post on X, BJP leader Pradeep Bhandari said India would have been sidelined on the global diplomatic stage had the Congress remained in power, citing the country's membership of BRICS and its position in international forums.He also accused the Congress of having "gifted" the United Nations Security Council seat to China during its tenure and criticised the party's handling of relations with Pakistan.The BJP leader further referred to the 1962 India-China war, blaming former Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru's China policy for the conflict."India does not need lectures from Congress which designed India's foreign policy keeping Pakistan Prem at centre!" the BJP leader wrote.- EndsMust Watch

news.title: Through the Lens: From ASEAN in Manila to APEC in Shenzhen
news.text:
The annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit concluded Thursday in Shenzhen, China, bringing together leaders from 21 economies, including Japan, the U.S. and China.

Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin for their first trilateral meeting. With Xi in the center, the three leaders walked side by side before sitting down for talks at a round table, projecting an image of coordination among the major powers.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen for the APEC summit on Wednesday. While many other leaders were greeted at the airport by honor guards and groups of young performers, Takaichi was welcomed by an honor guard only. China's Foreign Ministry said the host country had made appropriate ceremonial arrangements for all participants in accordance with international practice.

Earlier in the week, the Philippine capital of Manila took center stage in Asian diplomacy as leaders from the region and beyond gathered for three days of meetings at the 49th ASEAN Summit.

The meetings concluded Tuesday, with East Timor participating as the Southeast Asian bloc's newest member. Singapore will take over as ASEAN chair in 2027.

Trump arrived in Manila on the final day amid protests against his visit and the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative.

news.title: Asian American women feel the impact of Nvidia CEO affair scandal and 'spy' accusations
news.text:
The reveal earlier this month that billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs sent shock waves through the tech world, particularly with Asian Americans who revered him as a once-in-a-generation talent. But what has hit hard for Asian American women is the discourse around the allegation that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal, was possibly a spy. 

Almost immediately, videos and memes reviving tired tropes fetishizing Asian women hit social media.

“So few Asian women in general make it to the news for positive things. This is just going to continue to perpetuate negative stereotypes or biases for Asian women," said Misa Chien, founder of a network for Asian American women leaders called The Authentic Asian. Whether or not the allegation is true, “just the news will definitely influence people's opinions of women who have broken the ceiling or are trying to.”

Asian American women working in tech, civil rights advocacy and academia have felt a sense of dread that this ordeal will diminish how their peers are viewed and treated in their workplaces. It's a reminder that no accomplishments will completely dispel centuries-old stereotypes.

Jensen Huang has since resigned. However, the U.S. Justice Department has not found sufficient evidence that Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, was a spy. 

“I don’t know if that’s been determined yet," President Donald Trump told reporters this week.

 Asian women struggle to be taken seriously as leaders 

Among the social media posts being spread was a collage of photos showing CEOs with Asian female partners. Author May-lee Chai, who has written about the treatment of Asian women throughout history, called it “disgusting.”

Depicting them like trophy wives "implicates these spouses like they’re somehow similar to this suspected spy,” said Chai, a creative writing professor at San Francisco State University.

The speed at which people glommed onto the Asian female spy narrative was shocking to April Moh, chief marketing officer for a financial technology company and board member of Stand with Asian Americans, a legal civil rights organization specializing in combating workplace anti-Asian discrimination. The chatter has also led to women sharing stories of uncomfortable interactions. 

“I have women in technology who tell me that they get really weird looks and they get questioned about laptop security by their colleagues when they’re visiting China,” Moh said. “I have another person telling me that she has been jokingly asked, ‘So, are you a spy?’ by people who think that’s a joke now. It’s not funny to her or me.”

Many clients of Stand with Asian Americans are Asian women who have proved their competence yet are still accused of being fraudulent or deceitful, said Rachel Lee, the organization's president and general counsel. 

"It is deeply disturbing to see this not just unique to the Nvidia Jensen Huang case, but as a part of a long-standing dangerous narrative that Asians are perpetual foreigners, untrustworthy, disloyal,” Lee said. 

On top of their integrity being questioned, Asian workers also deal with misconceptions that they cannot lead. The annual Social Tracking of Asian Americans in the United States Index from The Asian American Foundation found at least half of U.S. adults characterized Asian Americans in the workplace as “respectful” or “reliable.” Only 1 in 10 viewed them as “assertive.”

“The No. 1 theme in onboarding interviews all last week were 'I’m mistaken for the secretary, I don’t look like the typical face of leadership," said Chien, talking about new members of her Asian leaders network.

 Stereotypes around Asian women go back centuries 

Years before Chinese laborers were fully banned from entering the U.S. under the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act, the federal government targeted immigrant Asian women. In 1875, Congress passed the Page Act to control immigration from “any Oriental country.” It included a specific prohibition of women coming for prostitution.

“Chinese women were deemed — and East Asian women in general — as being untrustworthy," Chai said. "It was presumed that they would be coming for illicit means as prostitutes to the United States and that would cause harm to white men.”

By the early 20th century, the Asian woman as a seductress, spy or “dragon lady” started becoming an archetype on Hollywood screens, she added. 

The headlines had Chien reflecting on when she played a spy in a building security ad in Hong Kong 20 years ago. She was instructed to wear three bras to resemble Angelina Jolie's figure. She wrote an Instagram post to point out “how the media enjoys putting Asian women in that kind of role" and urged women to not let people's assumptions keep them from success. 

“So many followers messaged me saying ‘thank you so much for speaking up,’" Chien said. 

 Real harm can come from stereotypes 

Suspicion toward Chinese people in the U.S. has dramatically heightened geopolitical tensions. Over two dozen states in the last few years have proposed or enacted “alien land laws” to prevent Chinese nationals from buying property. The number of international students enrolling in American universities has fallen. And the first Trump administration created a plan known as the " China Initiative " to crack down on espionage by profiling Chinese professors. 

Critics say that initiative contributed to the 2024 suicide of Jane Ying Wu. A neuroscientist at Northwestern University who had lived in the U.S. for 40 years, the 60-year-old came under federal investigation in 2019. She was never charged with anything. 

“This type of pernicious stereotype can actually destroy lives,” Chai said. “It’s not in any way an accurate portrait of an entire race and ethnicity.”

Jokes rooted in stereotypes under the guise of being complimentary also do not help Asian female workers, Lee added.

"Whether it’s a compliment or not, a trope is a trope,” she said. “I don’t care if it comes out of the mouth of the U.S. president.”

Ideally, Lee said more companies should allow for education and training around the harm and history of stereotypes. She encourages any woman who has had uncomfortable interactions to reach out to advocacy groups such as Stand with Asian Americans if she has nobody to turn to at work. At Stand with Asian Americans, people do not need to have a legal case of discrimination or harassment to receive assistance including education on their rights and mental health support. 

Individuals also have the right to draw boundaries and make clear what's not OK to say, Lee added. It's in employers' best interest to make sure no federal laws against discrimination and harassment are being violated.

“It's a win-win to have that conversation,” Lee said.

news.title: 2028 Is Looking Like 2016 but Upside Down
news.text:
The two parties' presidential lineups look a lot like those of the 2015-16 cycle — in reverse.

Republicans emerged from the 2014 midterm elections with large congressional majorities (247 House members and 54 senators). Democrats have emerged from this year's midterm elections with even larger ones (259 House members and 56 senators).

But Democrats then, like Republicans now, had a much smaller field of prospective presidential candidates. Two figures in former President Barack Obama's party towered over the others in visibility and popularity — his vice president, Joe Biden, and his first-term secretary of state, Hillary Clinton.

Recent vice presidents had won the presidency or come close, among them Richard Nixon, Hubert Humphrey, George H.W. Bush and Al Gore. No former secretary of state had won the presidency since James Buchanan in 1856. Yet Obama favored Clinton over Biden.

One reason may have been age. Clinton would have been 69 at the outset of the next presidential term, while Biden would have been 74. That didn't prevent Biden from becoming the consensus choice for the nomination four years later. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who was 75 by the next inauguration, was even older. He entered the primaries from stage left, winning 22 primaries and caucuses and holding Clinton to a 55 percent-43 percent advantage in votes cast for the nomination.

Today's Republican field looks as small as the Democratic field did at the same point in that cycle. It, too, includes a vice president and a secretary of state, with room for a third candidate who is no one's idea of a Washington insider.

Vice President JD Vance is in his first term, while Biden was in his second, and Vance's two years in the Senate pale beside Biden's 36. But Vance has the advantage of youth. He will be just 44 on Inauguration Day in 2029. Like Clinton, Secretary of State Marco Rubio served in the Senate — 14 years in his case, eight in hers. If elected in 2028, he would take the presidential oath at the mature but hardly elderly age of 57.

Rubio's statement that he won't run if Vance does can be read as an attempt to avoid turmoil in the Trump administration — a predictably unattainable goal. In the two weeks since the election, Vance has attributed the Republican rout solely to military action against Iran, which Rubio has supported. President Donald Trump, in turn, has publicly ordered Vance to give his full attention to exposing Democratic corruption in large cities.

Trump's favor may shift, and it may count for less than it once did. The Republican polling firm Echelon Insights reports that 56 percent of Republicans see themselves as party-first and only 36 percent as Trump-first. Another 51 percent say it is time to "move beyond the Trump approach."

The RealClearPolitics average of seven polls on the Republican nomination this fall shows Vance leading Rubio by a less-than-overwhelming margin, 37 percent to 28 percent. Outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL) draws 10 percent.

DeSantis' record of policy success in Florida, the only one of the 10 largest states to remain safely Republican this year, could make him a serious contender. He would be just 50 on Inauguration Day in 2029.

Meanwhile, Democrats, still giddy over their success, could field as many presidential candidates as the 10 Republicans who competed in the 2016 caucuses and primaries. That Republican field included senators from Florida, Kentucky and Texas; current and former governors from Arkansas, Florida, New Jersey and Ohio; a pediatric surgeon from Maryland; a former tech CEO from California; and a real estate developer and reality TV host from New York.

Trump won that crowded contest despite taking positions on trade, war and economic policy far outside those of previous Republican presidents. By the time he won an outright majority in any state, 36 states had already voted.

The Democratic field now taking shape looks something like that Republican field. The RealClearPolitics average of recent polls shows measurable support for 10 candidates. They include governors from California, Illinois, Kentucky and Pennsylvania, senators from Arizona, Georgia and New Jersey, a House member from New York, a former transportation secretary, and former Vice President Kamala Harris, the party's 2024 nominee.

They range widely in age and experience. If Harris took the presidential oath in January 2029, she would be the eighth-oldest person to do so for the first time. Just days would separate her from Zachary Taylor and George H.W. Bush. Only William Henry Harrison, Buchanan, Ronald Reagan, Trump and Biden were older than all three when they first took office. At the other end of the list, either Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), at 41, or Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY-14), at 39, would be the youngest president ever.

The field could grow or shrink. Someone whose candidacy seems as improbable as Trump's did a dozen years ago could enter the race and win.

America's two political parties have retained their basic characters across centuries. The Republican Party has always centered on people who see themselves, and whom others see, as typical Americans. In a nation that has always been culturally diverse, they have never made up a majority on their own.

The Democrat Party has always been a coalition of outsiders, people who see themselves, and whom others see, as outside the American mainstream. If they hold together, they can form a majority.

When Democrats lack a dominant leader — and Obama, nearly 10 years out of office, no longer seems to play that role — the danger is that the party's disparate constituencies will extract concessions that help candidates win the nomination but cost them votes in the general election.

Transgender advocates' demand for sex-change surgery for prisoners, which Harris docilely endorsed on camera, wounded her candidacy in 2024, perhaps fatally. Other demands from the period Ocasio-Cortez called "Woke 1" included defunding the police, admitting all otherwise illegal aliens who claim asylum, allowing biological men in girls' sports and women's prisons, and requiring masks during the COVID-19 pandemic. Endorsing such demands may help candidates win support in the spring 2028 primaries but prove disastrous in the general election.

Democrats will have a hard time balancing public demands for "affordability" with calls for more public spending from teachers unions and victims' groups. Continued demands for racial quotas and preferences in hiring and political districting may also seem beside the point. The country elected a black president in 2008, and voters just elected a Black Democrat senator in Mississippi and a Black Republican governor in Florida.

In days of yore, local Democratic bosses could grant concessions on some issues and mollify those whose demands they rejected. Today, the very existence of single-issue groups — and their payrolls — depends on wresting concessions from the party on unpopular issues. Popular positions usually don't need paid advocates.

As analysts have noted, most voters in the electorate that gave Democrats large majorities still view the party unfavorably. In the midterm elections, voters could use Democrats as a check on an increasingly disconnected Trump without giving the party full control of the government. In 2028, Democrats will ask for just that, while voters will likely see little risk of Republicans winning the presidency and both chambers of Congress, as they did in 2016 and 2024.

That's why Brookings scholars Elaine Kamarck and William Galston, who have been giving Democrats good advice for more than 30 years, write that "the midterms say little about who will win in 2028" and "do not conclusively show which kind of Democrat would be more electable at the national level in 2028."

Democrats are fortunate that their majorities are large enough to limit the leverage of the Democratic Socialists of America and other leftists in setting policy. But the left has a cheering section in the press and among affluent college graduates, who lately have been the party's largest constituency. Both groups will likely push the party leftward.

None of this is set in stone. Choices yet to be made and events yet to occur will shape the outcome, as they did 10 years ago. Democrats have an opportunity to present an attractive face, but they have flubbed such opportunities before. Republicans, for all their drubbing this year, still have assets that Trump, busy redesigning the White House complex and cleaning the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, has left undeployed.

Michael Barone is a senior political analyst for the Washington Examiner, resident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and longtime co-author of The Almanac of American Politics. His new book, "Mental Maps of the Founders: How Geographic Imagination Guided America's Revolutionary Leaders," is now available.

news.title: The Vice President Abandons His Deal
news.text:
On Wednesday morning, JD Vance was supposed to open Andrew Ross Sorkin's conference in New York. Thirty minutes before he was due on stage, Sorkin was told the vice president would not be coming because he had to stay in Washington. Within the hour, a "senior administration official" was briefing reporters on background about the string of outages that had taken down websites, bank portals, and back-end systems across the country. The vice president of the United States, given the chance to reassure the nation on stage and on camera, chose to do it on background.

The day before, Marco Rubio had already done it on the record. The secretary of state and national security adviser was in Asia with President Donald Trump. After 24 to 48 hours of Americans asking where the administration was, Rubio held an impromptu press conference, acknowledged that people were nervous, told them what the government knew, and said the government had "a duty to report that to the American people." It was the sort of thing Reagan, Bush, Clinton, and Obama used to do themselves.

The New York Times reports the president is frustrated with Vance for trying to put distance between himself and the president on Iran. The day after the midterms, Vance declared that the reason Republicans lost was the war. The president has since pulled him off the Iran talks and retasked him to focus on fraud.

The reassignment is interesting because Vance negotiated the memorandum of understanding with Iran. It was his deal. He led the American negotiating team, sat at the table and came home with the terms. Asked on Fox News this week whether there was any daylight between him and the president, Vance insisted there was none. He is overselling how like-minded the two men are on Iran, just as he oversold the memorandum of understanding.

His most devoted supporters have noticed the problem. A notable phenomenon has taken hold on social media, where Vance's fans insist the memorandum of understanding belongs to the president and was never really negotiated by the vice president. They are rewriting the story to protect the vice president from the fallout of the deal he negotiated.

Multiple Republican senators have told me the same thing. Support for the memorandum of understanding and for how the administration handled Iran was high at first with Republicans. Then those same Republicans found out what was actually in the memorandum. Once they did, even their support for the war turned decisively against the deal. That collapse came after the vice president negotiated the deal, and it came because of what he negotiated.

Consider where that leaves the administration.

The president is aggravated with his vice president. The vice president no longer wants ownership of a memorandum of understanding with a terrorist nation — a memorandum he negotiated himself. The secretary of state, jet-lagged and juggling China, Russia, and Iran, has become the face of the administration and the president cannot stop praising him. "How hot is Marco, right?" the president asked at the ASEAN summit in Manila.

Politicians have always run from their failures, but it is rarer to watch a vice president run from his own signature. Vance wants to inherit the president's coalition in 2028. A man who wants to lead the party, however, cannot negotiate the most consequential foreign policy agreement of the term and then pretend he had nothing to do with it.

Scripture tells us to let our yes be yes, and our no be no. A man who says yes at the negotiating table should not say no on social media when the deal turns unpopular, and he should not hide behind a background briefing when the country wants to hear from its leaders.

The 2028 conversations are already happening, with donors fielding calls and would-be candidates surveying their lanes. Republican primary voters are going to remember who stood in front of the cameras when Americans needed reassurance and who briefed reporters as a nameless official. Unfortunately for the vice president, they are also going to remember whose signature is on the deal with Iran that dragged out a war instead of ending it.

news.title: Goodbye Electoral College, Hello Totalitarianism, Part One
news.text:
As we all know, the Democratic Party wants to abolish the Electoral College (EC). They might make a big push in the next two years to do so, and it is not impossible that they will succeed. Most Americans are totally clueless about why our Founders established the Electoral College, a matter I will fully discuss in part two of this series. The Democrats are trying to make it all about “democracy” now — which, in one sense, it is, and they might be able to demagogue enough people into abolishing the EC.

Technically, since the Electoral College is part of the election process and ensconced in the Constitution, the Democrats would need a constitutional amendment to abolish it. Technically. In this regard, the problem for them is that they would need 38 states to ratify the amendment, and they almost assuredly don’t have that many at present, and it will probably be several years, at best, before they could muster that number. Most Southern and Western states (minus the Left Coast) would not go for the abolition of the EC by constitutional amendment. So, the Democrats have decided to try an end run around the EC.

They have created this monstrosity called the “National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.” This thing has been around for well over a decade now, and it might be gaining steam. The idea is to find a way to elect the president by popular vote and bypass the EC (if it can’t be eradicated by constitutional amendment). What the NPVIC says is that any state would give all its electoral votes to the candidate who received the most national popular votes, even if that candidate did not win that state’s popular vote. For example, if candidate “A” won the national popular vote, he would get all of a state’s electoral votes even if candidate “B” actually won the state’s popular vote. The state’s “electors” would then be required to vote for candidate “A” when the Electoral College voted on the president. If enough states adopt the NPVIC, the Electoral College, as constitutionally construed, would be negated and bypassed.

So far, 18 states, all (unsurprisingly) very blue, and representing 222 electoral votes, have joined this compact. The newly elected Democrat governor of Nevada, Aaron Ford, hopes to get his state to enact the NPVIC. He has said that the Electoral College must go because it has “racist underpinnings,” and “not only for that reason but because we’ve seen several times now the person who wins the popular vote not win [the presidency] because of the Electoral College.” The Democrats will push this “national popular vote” thing — “the people should decide by popular vote who the president will be.” That’s the approach they are going to hammer — and already are, and it will persuade millions of Americans who, as I said, have absolutely no idea why the Founding Fathers established the Electoral College. And the Left isn’t going to tell them; that’s for sure.

I don’t know if Aaron Ford is just ignorant, or if he is being dishonest in what he said. To claim the EC had “racist underpinnings” is utterly ridiculous historically (but he’s a Democrat and, of course, for Democrats, everything they don’t like is “racist”), and when he said that several times the person who won the popular vote wasn’t elected president because of the Electoral College, he shows total ignorance of why our Founders established the EC, or, if he does know, he’s being very disingenuous. My guess is, like most Americans, he just doesn’t know the first thing about what our Founders did, or why.

There have indeed been five instances in American history (1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, and 2016) when the person who received the most popular votes did not become president because an opponent won the Electoral College vote (or, in 1824, a vote in the House of Representatives, which chooses the president if no candidate wins in the EC). Note especially the dates above — among them 2000, when Al Gore won the popular vote, but George Bush became president, and 2016, when Hillary Clinton received more popular votes than Donald Trump (maybe). The latter, especially, sticks in Democrats' craw. Trump did get more popular votes in 2024 than Kamala Harris, but under a “election by popular vote” system, Hillary would have won in 2016. The Democrats, of course, want to, and will when they can, invite millions more illegals into the country, give them amnesty and citizenship as soon as possible, and thus the right to vote. To Democrats, the abolition (or bypassing) of the Electoral College, and a president elected solely by national popular vote, would put them in power as far into the future as foreseeable. And, if they have their way on the EC, immigration, and amnesty, they are probably right about that. America would become a one-party, totalitarian state.

One reason our Founders established the Electoral College was to prevent totalitarianism in America. My next article in this series will explain exactly what they did, and why.

news.title: Zelensky lied when he said that coalition supported Ukraine’s NATO membership — MP
news.text:
MOSCOW, November 20. /TASS/. Vladimir Zelensky lied when he said that participants of the Coalition of the Willing, who gathered in Berlin, supported Ukraine’s accession to NATO, Ukrainian lawmaker Alexander Dubinsky said.

The meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, organized by the UK, Germany and France, took place in the German capital on Thursday. Zelensky told reporters after the talks that the partners supported NATO and EU membership for Ukraine.

"Zelensky lied again when he claimed that members of the Coalition of the Willing supported Ukraine’s accession to NATO," the lawmaker wrote on Telegram. "The German government’s official statement on the outcomes of the summit mentions only security guarantees and continued support for Ukraine, and there is not a single word about NATO membership."

Furthermore, according to the RBC-Ukraine news agency, Zelensky told reporters after the talks that the US side, together with European partners, is prepared to offer Kiev security guarantees modeled on NATO’s Article 5. At the same time, he acknowledged that the parties lack a shared understanding on what such guarantees will mean in practice. In Zelensky’s words, he is unsure if everyone interprets Article 5 the same way.

Kiev has repeatedly expressed its desire to become a full-fledged member of the North Atlantic Alliance as soon as possible. In September 2022, Ukraine submitted a fast-track application to join NATO. In January 2025, Zelensky complained that Hungary, Germany, Slovakia, and the US opposed Ukraine’s NATO membership. In March 2025, US President Donald Trump remarked that the answer to Ukraine’s aspiration to join the alliance is well-known. According to him, Ukrainians have known this answer for the past 40 years.
news.summary: Alexander Dubinsky noted that Germany’s statement on the outcomes of the summit of the Coalition of the Willing "mentions only security guarantees and continued support for Ukraine"

news.title: Trump DOJ Abruptly Drops 'Two Sullivans' Alaska Fight After Peltola Win
news.text: The Trump administration on Thursday moved to abandon its legal bid to block certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, telling a federal appeals court that "this case is moot." In a filing with the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, Justice Department lawyers asked the judges to declare the case over and to wipe away the lower-court ruling that had already thrown it out. The retreat came two days after the Associated Press called the race for Peltola, who won an outright majority of first-choice votes over two-term Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The lawsuit was built for a photo finish. Alaska delivered something else. A case designed to freeze a razor-thin result now had nothing left to freeze, and the department said as much. The fight over the race is not entirely over. A federal criminal investigation into the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., the retired Petersburg schoolteacher who shared the senator's name on the ballot, is continuing, Attorney General Todd Blanche has said. And Sullivan has not posted publicly since the race was called. Why the Justice Department Is Dropping Its Alaska Senate Lawsuit The department sued Alaska election officials on October 22, after President Donald Trump ordered the case. "I'm the one that said 'do it,'" he later said. The suit turned on a single scenario: Sullivan losing, but by fewer votes than his namesake received. In that event, the department wanted certification blocked until investigators could determine whether voters who chose Sullivan Jr. had meant to choose the senator. Its lawyers warned that a narrow Peltola win would be a "tainted victory." The administration never explained how such an inquiry could work without breaching the secret ballot. U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the case on November 1, two days before the election, ruling that the federal government lacked standing and that setting ballots aside would violate the secret ballot. The department appealed the same day. Lawyers from Alaska's Department of Law, representing the state's election officials, had urged the judge to toss it, calling the suit meritless. Even before the votes were counted, Newsweek noted that a clear Peltola win would likely make the lawsuit moot, since the request hinged on a Sullivan loss. The department's response to a pending motion at the 9th Circuit was due Thursday. It answered by folding its hand, while asking the court to vacate Gleason's ruling on the way out. It is at least the second time since Election Day that the department has moved to drop a high-profile election lawsuit. The first targeted roughly 20,000 California ballots it said were cast by suspected noncitizens. Is the 'Decoy Dan' Criminal Investigation Over? No. The civil suit is collapsing, but the criminal investigation it traveled alongside remains open. Federal prosecutors are investigating whether Democrats recruited Sullivan Jr. to siphon votes from the incumbent. On Election Day, they sent target letters to several people, including Marc Elias, whose firm represents Peltola's campaign. Elias said the department was "targeting me and my law firm on Election Day." No one has been charged. It remains unclear whether recruiting a namesake candidate would break any criminal law. Ballot stacking is not illegal at the federal level, and the department has not said which offenses it is examining. The Justice Department did not respond to questions from Newsweek on Wednesday about whether the race being called changes anything about the investigation. Peltola has denied any role in Sullivan Jr.'s candidacy, and he has long said the decision to run was his own. Trump has demanded that Peltola be prosecuted. After the call, House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said the outright majority "will probably create issues" for the Justice Department, but added, "I think there is still a case," in an interview with NewsNation. A separate state inquiry, ordered by Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, is also open. "The Alaska Bureau of Investigation continues to investigate allegations related to the Alaska US Senate election," Austin McDaniel, a deputy commissioner at the state Department of Public Safety, told Newsweek on Wednesday. What Peltola and Sullivan Have Said Peltola, who would be the first Alaska Native in the Senate, has kept her eyes forward. "Thank you, Alaska. Let's get to work," she wrote on X after the race was called. She has since said it is time to move on and that she wants to work for all Alaskans. Sullivan has not conceded. On Monday, his campaign said it would let the process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified, and promised to say more by the end of the week. What Comes Next: Alaska Senate Certification and Swearing-In With the Justice Department backing off, the path to Washington runs through a short calendar. Under the Division of Elections schedule: Peltola would take the oath when the new Congress convenes on January 3, 2027.
news.summary: Trump’s DOJ drops its ‘Decoy Dan’ lawsuit to block Mary Peltola’s Alaska Senate win, calling it moot. The criminal probe goes on.
news.author: Lars Hanson

news.title: Texas Launches Audit of Senate Race Results after Democratic Sweep
news.text: Texas election officials this week launched the state's first risk-limiting audit, a post-election review designed to verify the outcome of a statewide race using randomly selected paper ballots. The audit is the first held under a law passed by the Texas Legislature in 2021, following years of pilot programs before becoming mandatory for statewide elections held after August 31, 2026. It just happens to coincide with the "blue tsunami" seen across the country. "We've had five years to pilot this program, and we're very excited to finally kick it off and do this for the first time," Christina Adkins, director of elections for the Office of the Texas Secretary of State, said at the audit launch event Wednesday. The review is not a recount prompted by allegations of fraud or evidence of errors. Instead, it is intended to provide statistical evidence that the reported outcome of a statewide contest matches the votes cast by Texans, officials said. "Texans deserve to know their elections are secure and their votes are counted accurately," Robert Howden, Texas secretary of state, said in a statement announcing the audit. "We have multiple checks and balances throughout the process and now we have two ways to verify the results after the election." How Much Did James Talarico Win By? One of the races being audited is the Texas Senate race. According to the Texas Secretary of State, Democrat James Talarico defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton by about 1.19 million votes, or 12 percentage points. Paxton was considered a problematic candidate with a history of scandals and allegations of wrongdoing, but he was President Donald Trump's pick over incumbent Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary. Neither has made a public comment about the audit. Newsweek reached out to both Talarico and Paxton's offices for comment. What We Know About the Audit Risk-limiting audits have become increasingly popular among election administrators in recent years because they use physical ballots rather than electronic vote totals to verify election outcomes. The process is already used in 16 states, according to the Texas Secretary of State's office. The introduction of statewide risk-limiting audits in Texas stems from Senate Bill 598, which was approved by the Texas Legislature and signed into law in 2021. The measure directed the secretary of state to develop procedures for statistically verifying election outcomes using paper ballots. The process begins with a random selection of ballots generated using publicly observable procedures, which was the roll of 20 10-sided dice for Texas. Counties will now spend this week manually reviewing those ballots and comparing them to the reported results. If the sample provides sufficient statistical confidence that the outcome is correct, the audit concludes. If not, additional ballots can be examined. Under Texas law, a full hand recount may ultimately be ordered if necessary. Texas has previously conducted other forms of election audits, including local hand-count reviews of selected precincts and broader county audits examining election administration practices. "The addition of statewide risk-limiting audits is an important milestone for Texas elections," Howden said. "It gives an additional layer of accountability and transparency into the process." Election experts generally view risk-limiting audits as one of the strongest methods available for confirming election outcomes without conducting a full statewide recount. Supporters argue that the audits can strengthen public confidence by providing an independent review of paper ballots while avoiding the time and expense of recounting every vote. Texas law requires the secretary of state to make the results publicly available within days of the audit's completion. Officials said results will be posted on the website. Former CBS correspondent Lara Logan called the risk-limiting audit "worse than useless" in an X post in response to Texas' announcement. "Republicans who won their races in Texas should be calling for a full 100 percent paper audit - not a risk-limiting audit that only looks at a fraction of the votes. They should also be calling for an investigation to verify the legitimacy of the voters who cast ballots in the midterms. That would include a “digital canvas” which would compare state voter registration databases, voter check-in lists, voter histories & the cast vote record from this election to existing government & private databases to verify citizenship status, addresses & so on," she wrote on X. Conservative activist and podcaster Joe Oltmann, who has promoted disputed claims about the 2020 election, also criticized the Texas review as inadequate. “A dice roll is not an audit. Hand count the whole race and publish every chain of custody record," he wrote. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. news.summary: A state law makes Texas' 2026 midterm election the first to undergo a risk-limiting audit.

news.title: German lawmaker describes Putin-Trump-Xi meeting as historic
news.text:
BERLIN, November 20. /TASS/. The meeting of Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in China’s Shenzhen is historic because even the fact that dialogue has begun among the leaders of the major powers holds diplomatic value, said Steffen Kotre, a Bundestag member from the Alternative for Germany (AfD) faction and the party’s energy policy expert.

"[I view this meeting] as historic: the leaders of the three major countries are coming together and talking to one another," he told TASS. "In diplomacy, the very fact that dialogue has begun is already of value."

The lawmaker emphasized that trust, which takes a long time to build, is the foundation of everything.

"In doing so, the leaders of the three countries are sending a positive signal, in contrast to the Europeans, who are banking on confrontation and rejection of diplomacy," he said.

Putin, Xi Jinping, and Trump held a meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, the first such meeting ever. The heads of state exchanged views on the current international situation and expressed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security.

The leaders also adopted a declaration on peace. They expressed support for reforming the UN to ensure a more effective response to the global challenges. According to the document, Russia, China, and the United States plan to increase the production and supply of petroleum products for the benefit of all countries. It is noted that respect for the immunities of state officials is of fundamental importance, and the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers. The leaders emphasized that a nuclear war must never be unleashed - there will be no winners in it. It is also noted that Russia, China, and the United States will engage in dialogue to reduce nuclear risks.
news.summary: The fact that dialogue has begun among the leaders of the major powers holds diplomatic value, Steffen Kotre, a Bundestag member from the Alternative for Germany faction, said

news.title: Byron Donalds Says 2028 Hopefuls Must Define Themselves, Rules Out Own Bid
news.text: Byron Donalds, Republican congressman and incoming Florida governor, said that 2028 hopefuls will need to redefine their own coalitions and not recreate the previous administrations. “To be blunt: What I’ve observed in politics, it’s very hard for somebody to try to recreate the previous person’s coalition,” Donalds told Politico at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in part on Thursday. Donalds made history as Florida's first Black governor to be elected to office. President Donald Trump threw his support behind Donalds as did Florida Governor Ron DeSantis after the primary. Following devastating midterm election losses for Republicans, which resulted in losing both House and Senate majority, speculation has swirled surrounding who will be the successor to MAGA after Trump is out of office. DeSantis' post-midterm media rounds have sparked intrigue into whether he is considering another bid for the White House. He was asked about a potential 2028 run by CNN's Jake Tapper after Election Day and said in part that he has not "planned anything." Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Glenn Youngkin, former Republican governor of Virginia, and many more have all been asked about their intentions for running in 2028 on the Republican side. Similarly, Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and many more have also been asked about their political futures on the Democratic side. What To Know During his conversation with Politico's Adam Wren, Donalds said that “Whoever the next person is going to be, they’re going to have to — in some respects — redefine and reshape the electorate about what their supportive coalition is.“ "I think trying to go back into trying to recreate what somebody else’s success was, I think is foolhardy,” he added. Donalds was asked by Politico if his comments were aimed at Vance, and he responded in part that it is "just the reality of politics,” and running on someone else's coalition "rarely works." “I would advise anybody who’s thinking about taking the next step: You got to define yourself,” Donalds also told the outlet on Thursday. “You have to be yourself. You can’t be a facsimile or a carbon copy or shades of gray of somebody else.” Following the midterm losses, Trump administration officials speculated on why the results unfolded in such a bruising manner. Vance said that after speaking with a pollster, four areas jumped out, including ending the war with Iran, focusing on the cost of living and inflation, putting America first and changing America's relationship with Israel. Trump was asked if he had spoken with Vance about 2028 after the midterms and said in part earlier this month, "We'll see what happens. ... You don't know who's talking about running. ... Maybe he won't run, I don't know who's gonna run." Last month, Vance said he thought the president would endorse him should he launch an official 2028 campaign but added they had not discussed it. Donalds also shot down any potential 2028 run for himself saying to Politico that he is "absolutely" shutting the door on it, adding "it is not happening." “I take this job very seriously,” he later added. “I am not looking at another one.” Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Thursday, "Donalds is saying the obvious out loud. Coalitions are personal. Trump’s is built around him. [Former President Barack] Obama’s was built around him. Trying to photocopy either one usually fails. The next Republican nominee will have to assemble something that fits their own strengths and the electorate of 2028, not 2024. That is basic politics, not a break with Trump. "His quick no on running himself is also practical. He just won Florida. He has a full term ahead, a legislature to manage, and a record to build. Jumping into a national primary before he has governed would look premature to most voters and donors," Agranoff added. "It keeps the focus on the job he just got and leaves the 2028 field open for others who are already positioning. It is the kind of clear answer that avoids speculation without creating new problems." What Prediction Markets Show On prediction market Kalshi Thursday night, Vance has a 33 percent chance of winning the GOP presidential nomination. Rubio has 22 percent and DeSantis has 16 percent. On Polymarket, Vance has 33 percent Thursday night, Rubio has 21 percent, DeSantis has 15 percent and other potential candidates, including Cruz, Youngkin and Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, all have single digits. news.summary: Donalds says that he plans to keep his focus on running the state of Florida.

news.title: ‘Nuclear War Must Never Be Fought’: Trump, Xi And Putin Sign Joint Declaration At Historic Summit
news.text:
The leaders of the United States, Russia and China signed a joint “peace declaration” at an unprecedented trilateral summit on Thursday, agreeing that nuclear war must never be fought. However, the high-profile meeting ended without any concrete commitment to the arms control negotiations that US President Donald Trump has long advocated.
The declaration, signed by Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, marked the culmination of Trump's three-day diplomatic tour of Asia.
What Trump, Xi And Putin Agreed On
The joint declaration outlined areas of agreement among the three nuclear powers, including the need to prevent nuclear conflict, expand petroleum production and reform international institutions.
The leaders reiterated that “nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought”. They also expressed their intention to increase petroleum production and supply, as per reports.
On international governance, the declaration said the three countries were “committed to reform the UN” to make it more effective in addressing global challenges.
The statement also raised concerns about the immunity enjoyed by government officials, noting that “they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”.

Trump Calls China Visit ‘Great And Highly Consequential’
Trump described his diplomatic engagements in China as a major success while travelling back to Washington aboard Air Force One.
In a social media post, he called the visit “a great and highly consequential trip” and announced that he would address the media at a White House news conference on Friday.
During the visit, Trump held separate meetings with Putin and Xi. His meeting with the Russian president was their first since August 2025, with Trump warmly greeting Putin as his “friend”.
He also described his relationship with Xi as “very special” following their separate conversation.
Xi And Putin Highlight Their Priorities
Despite the cordial atmosphere, the three leaders approached the summit with different diplomatic priorities.
Xi, in his opening remarks, emphasised the importance of cooperation among major global powers, saying that “positive interaction among major powers is not a matter of choice, but a mandatory requirement”.
Putin, meanwhile, stressed the shared interest in bringing the Ukraine war to an end. He also indicated that food and energy security would feature in the discussions.
Ukraine War Remains A Challenge For Beijing
China's position on the Russia-Ukraine conflict continues to be a key diplomatic consideration. Beijing has maintained that it is neutral since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
It has rejected allegations from Ukraine and its Western allies that it has indirectly supported Moscow by supplying dual-use technology that could be used by the Russian military.
China has repeatedly advocated negotiations and a political settlement without directly condemning Russia's military action.

Trump Calls For Nuclear Cooperation
In his closing remarks, Trump said the leaders of the three major powers had a “special responsibility” to maintain constructive communication despite their differences.
“Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements,” he said, adding: “We feel the opposite.”
Pointing to their nuclear capabilities, Trump argued that the three countries were “uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth”.
He also stressed the need for cooperation to “combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world”, adding: “That’s what we’re doing in Iran.”
