news.title: Chilling Image Captures the Moment Global Power Shifted
news.text:
A picture can speak volumes. Chinese President Xi Jinping ensured that plenty of cameras were present to record the moment when the balance of global power appeared to shift in public.

As Donald Trump shook hands with Vladimir Putin at the opening of the Apec summit in Shenzhen, Xi stood beside the two leaders, watching with an approving expression.

It was an unsettling image, made even more disturbing by the way the American president greeted Putin before the trilateral talks began.

‘Who is he?’ Trump asked rhetorically as he entered the room and saw the Russian leader, a pariah in the eyes of much of the Western world. Then he laughed and added: ‘He’s my friend!’

The remark provoked outrage among senior US figures on social media, who were appalled that Trump appeared to be pandering to an autocrat still waging a brutal invasion of another country.

‘Trump greeting Putin with such warmth is beyond nauseating,’ wrote Daniel Shapiro, the former US ambassador to Israel.

Xi, meanwhile, appeared to relish the scene as Trump humiliated not only himself before the cameras, but also America and the West, by openly courting Putin and China.

For decades after the end of the Second World War in 1945, the United States remained the world’s leading power, although Moscow occasionally challenged its position. China, by contrast, was desperately poor and wielded little influence.

At the summit, however, the American and Russian presidents were seated symbolically on either side of Xi, with one to his left and the other to his right.

They appeared less like equals than supplicants competing for the Chinese leader’s favour.

Who could have imagined an American president before Donald Trump allowing himself to become an extra at an international summit, rather than presiding as its host? Trump is plainly impressed by the idea of the ‘strong man’ and wants to project that image himself.

Xi, however, was not simply hosting the meeting. He appeared to be the dominant figure in the room, evoking images of the Chinese emperors who ruled for centuries when their empire was regarded as the ‘centre of the world’.

Under Xi, China’s Communist leadership is putting the country first.

Trump and Putin were portrayed as subordinate rulers who had come to seek the Chinese leader’s approval as they attempted to address their wars and trade disputes.

America is at war with Iran, while Russia remains locked in a devastating conflict with Ukraine. China, by comparison, stands at peace amid a world consumed by war.

Of course, Beijing has used the wars of other countries—particularly those involving America and Russia—to expand its influence around the globe.

Chinese weapons and technology have supported Russia’s brutal war in Ukraine, while intelligence assistance has been provided to Iran, an adversary of the United States.

Even so, Trump appeared willing to accept China’s backing for both Iran and Russia. ‘It’s an honour to be your friend,’ he told Xi in notably deferential terms.

The three leaders issued a ‘peace declaration’ after the summit, even as Putin’s war continues in Ukraine. As Trump’s critics on social media noted, the Russian army has been accused of slaughtering and raping women and abducting 20,000 children.

That declaration also came as China continued to expand its offensive capabilities on a frightening scale, issued increasingly aggressive warnings over Taiwan and carried out brazen espionage operations across the Western world.

There was no breakthrough on trade, nor were any major commercial agreements announced. Surprisingly, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that he and Xi had not discussed tariffs—the issue that caused widespread disruption when he imposed levies on Chinese and other foreign goods last year, before reaching a temporary truce.

China is one of America’s biggest trading partners and accounts for roughly a third of global manufacturing. Both economies would suffer if tensions escalated into a full-scale trade war.

But American voters are particularly sensitive to rising costs, and they would not welcome any new tariffs from Trump if those measures pushed up the price of Chinese imports.

The devastating midterm results exposed Trump’s vulnerability on that issue. Republicans lost long-held Senate strongholds, including Kansas, Texas and Alaska, after voters became angry over soaring petrol prices linked to the war with Iran.

Xi does not have to answer to voters. His relentless expansion of China’s manufacturing capacity—from low-cost plastics to higher-value products such as electric cars, refrigerators, televisions and computers—has helped propel him into a commanding position on the world stage.

Some advisers accompanying Trump are reportedly unhappy with the damaging optics of a visit that casts America as the world’s Number Two. Yet they appear willing to endure the situation for the remainder of Trump’s two-year term.

Two years is a long time for events to spiral out of control—especially when they seem to be drawing the United States towards China’s dark orbit.

news.title: Ten new books our critics have been reading. Are they any good?
news.text:
Reasoning With Chaos by Waleed Aly (Allen & Unwin, $35)Can you reason with chaos? This collection of newspaper columns is a real-time demonstration of one man’s attempt to wrangle meaning out of events that seem to defy reason. Charting a period of just over a year from the eve of Donald Trump’s second victory, these pieces are an implicit plea for reflection over reaction, for humility over outrage, for not letting fundamental principles – the right to protest, the sacred trust between health professionals and patients, the humanity of those we disagree with – be obscured by political righteousness.

Aly has a knack for seeing the bigger picture in the nitty-gritty of the immediate moment. When it emerges that overseas groups are funding criminals to carry out antisemitic attacks on Australian soil, he points to the profound implications for us all if violence is commoditised so that “nations and gangs alike can now, with similar ease, outsource attacks on their foes to something like the gig economy”. Even when the insights are grim or bracing, Aly’s cool-headedness offers a model for how to abide with, and make sense of, these febrile times.

The Culture Wars by Tim Dunlop (MUP, $30)“Political correctness”, “black armband history”, “woke”, “cancel culture” – these catchy pejoratives are the surface manifestations of what Tim Dunlop identifies as a conscious strategy by politicians since the 1970s to divide and conquer communities rather than bring them together. While all politicians use culture war tactics, he says, the conservative end of the spectrum has driven these debates because it needs to “align working-class voters with elite interests through appeals to shared cultural identity”.

Dunlop argues that debates about race, gender, religion, immigration, class, free trade, Indigenous rights and national identity have been with us since Federation. What has changed is the way they are weaponised. In forensic, snappy prose, he lays bare how political leaders on both sides unleashed neoliberal economics which turbocharged the culture wars. As Labor lost touch with its collectivist roots, Howard drove “a truck through the uncertainties the Hawke-Keating government helped create”. But that truck ultimately backfired on the Coalition and left it at war with itself.

Over the Rainbow edited by Drew Hutton and Libby Connors (Spinifex Press, $39.95)Does critiquing the ideology behind the transgender rights movement make you a “transphobe”? Does it mean you should be silenced and accused of hate speech? Have public institutions and environmental groups such as the Greens come under the sway of this ideology to the extent that it is deemed acceptable to cancel those who dissent? news.text:
Reasoning With Chaos by Waleed Aly (Allen & Unwin, $35)Can you reason with chaos? This collection of newspaper columns is a real-time demonstration of one man’s attempt to wrangle meaning out of events that seem to defy reason. Charting a period of just over a year from the eve of Donald Trump’s second victory, these pieces are an implicit plea for reflection over reaction, for humility over outrage, for not letting fundamental principles – the right to protest, the sacred trust between health professionals and patients, the humanity of those we disagree with – be obscured by political righteousness.

Aly has a knack for seeing the bigger picture in the nitty-gritty of the immediate moment. When it emerges that overseas groups are funding criminals to carry out antisemitic attacks on Australian soil, he points to the profound implications for us all if violence is commoditised so that “nations and gangs alike can now, with similar ease, outsource attacks on their foes to something like the gig economy”. Even when the insights are grim or bracing, Aly’s cool-headedness offers a model for how to abide with, and make sense of, these febrile times.

The Culture Wars by Tim Dunlop (MUP, $30)“Political correctness”, “black armband history”, “woke”, “cancel culture” – these catchy pejoratives are the surface manifestations of what Tim Dunlop identifies as a conscious strategy by politicians since the 1970s to divide and conquer communities rather than bring them together. While all politicians use culture war tactics, he says, the conservative end of the spectrum has driven these debates because it needs to “align working-class voters with elite interests through appeals to shared cultural identity”.

Dunlop argues that debates about race, gender, religion, immigration, class, free trade, Indigenous rights and national identity have been with us since Federation. What has changed is the way they are weaponised. In forensic, snappy prose, he lays bare how political leaders on both sides unleashed neoliberal economics which turbocharged the culture wars. As Labor lost touch with its collectivist roots, Howard drove “a truck through the uncertainties the Hawke-Keating government helped create”. But that truck ultimately backfired on the Coalition and left it at war with itself.

news.title: San Jose Mosque Incident Leads to Arrest of a Fresno Man
news.text:
A 38-year-old Fresno man was arrested after allegedly threatening several children inside a mosque in San Jose.

Hector Lopez was taken into custody Nov. 12 on suspicion of making criminal threats against a group of juveniles at the Evergreen Islamic Center, the San Jose Police Department said.

According to a preliminary investigation, Lopez entered the place of worship, threatened the children and left in a vehicle before officers arrived.

“With the assistance of SJPD Real Time Intelligence Center Analysts, Patrol Officers were able to utilize Automated License Plate Reader cameras to quickly locate the suspect vehicle,” the department said.

Officers identified Lopez and later found him. He was booked into the Santa Clara County Main Jail on suspicion of making criminal threats.

The incident was not the first time the mosque had reportedly been targeted.

In November 2016, the Evergreen Islamic Center was among six California Islamic centers that reportedly received threatening letters, according to SFGate.

The letter reportedly mentioned then-President-elect Donald Trump and claimed he would do to Muslims what “Hitler did to the Jews.”

Zahra Billoo, executive director of the Bay Area chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, urged the FBI to investigate the threats.

The California Post contacted the Evergreen Islamic Center and the San Jose Police Department for additional comment.

news.title: Dow Drops Below Pam Bondi Threshold of 50,000 as Nvidia Shares Slide
news.text: The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged more than 1,100 points Thursday, dropping below the now-infamous 50,000-point milestone Pam Bondi highlighted during her contentious congressional testimony on sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The decline marked the index's first close below that threshold since June, bringing renewed attention to a figure that became a political talking point earlier this year. Bondi, who was then attorney general, invoked the index's performance while facing questions from lawmakers about the Justice Department's handling of the Epstein investigation. “The Dow is over 50,000 ... I don't know why you're laughing. You're a great stock trader, as I hear, Raskin,” Bondi said, addressing Representative Jamie Raskin. At the time, Bondi was pointing to the index's record-breaking performance as evidence of the Trump administration's economic achievements. The blue-chip index lost 1,101.11 points, or 2.19 percent, to close at 49,097.06 on Thursday. The S&P 500 shed 2.02 percent to finish at 7,175.83, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite dropped 2.25 percent to close at 23,879.20. Thursday's sell-off came amid growing concerns about the artificial intelligence industry, regulatory oversight and the prospect of more aggressive Federal Reserve interest rate increases. Investors were closely watching Nvidia (NVDA), whose shares reversed early gains Thursday, sliding 3.3 percent to $145.98 despite the company's stronger-than-expected quarterly results earlier this week. The decline brought the stock back to levels last seen in late 2024. Why Pam Bondi's 50,000 Dow Remark Became a Political Talking Point The 50,000 milestone has an unusual connection to one of the most contentious congressional hearings of 2026. On February 11, Bondi appeared before the House Judiciary Committee as lawmakers questioned her about the Justice Department's handling of documents connected to Epstein, the disgraced financier. During the hearing, lawmakers pressed the attorney general about the release of Epstein-related records, the treatment of victims and whether the department was pursuing additional investigations. Bondi responded by defending the administration's handling of the documents and criticizing Democrats for focusing on Epstein. She then turned to the economy. “The S&P at almost 7,000, and the Nasdaq smashing records. Americans' 401(k)s and retirement savings are booming. That's what we should be talking about," Bondi said, arguing that Americans' 401(k) accounts and retirement savings were benefiting from the strong stock market. Her comments drew laughter from the committee, with lawmakers questioning the relevance of stock market performance to the subject of the hearing. Bondi nevertheless doubled down, celebrating the Dow's achievement and crediting President Donald Trump with reaching the milestone much earlier than critics had expected. The exchange became one of the most memorable moments of the hearing, linking the Dow's performance to a broader political debate about the administration's economic record. The 50,000 figure was never an official economic threshold. Rather, it became a symbolic benchmark after Bondi used it to defend the Trump administration during questioning about Epstein, the sex offender. Newsweek has reached out to Bondi for comment. Nvidia's Earnings Fail to Deliver a Lasting Rally Nvidia reported stronger-than-expected third-quarter results, initially giving investors reason for optimism. The upbeat report, however, failed to sustain momentum, with shares reversing course Thursday. The company reported adjusted earnings of $2.68 per share on revenue of $115.84 billion for the quarter ending October 25. Wall Street analysts had expected adjusted earnings of $2.48 per share on revenue of approximately $109 billion. Revenue increased 103 percent year over year, reinforcing the company's position at the center of the global artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. “Our momentum is real,” Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, told investors and financial analysts of the results. “Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us. And employees are committed. We’ve got this.” Investors were also considering a reported Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into whether Nvidia's disclosures may have misled investors, according to The Wall Street Journal. The reported inquiry adds another source of uncertainty for the chipmaker, which has also faced questions surrounding its leadership following reports involving former CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia's board has said it is not considering bringing Huang back. The combination of leadership uncertainty, regulatory scrutiny and concerns about the sustainability of AI spending has weighed on investor sentiment. When Did the Dow Last Fall Below 50,000? The Dow Jones Industrial Average first closed above 50,000 on February 6, 2026, finishing the session at 50,115.67. The achievement came after a volatile period for Wall Street, with investors increasingly concerned about artificial intelligence valuations, technology spending and the broader economic outlook. However, market data shows the index subsequently slipped below the milestone, closing at 49,451.98 on February 12 and 49,662.66 on February 18. It later recovered and climbed higher. By June, it had moved back above 50,000, and Thursday's close marked its first finish below the threshold since. The difference is that the Dow's February breakthrough was accompanied by a strong rally, while Thursday's decline came amid renewed uncertainty surrounding technology stocks, inflation and interest rates. Could Anthropic's IPO Lift the Stock Market Again? Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO offered another test of investor appetite for artificial intelligence companies. The company behind Claude made its stock market debut Thursday, with shares surging and briefly pushing its valuation above $2 trillion. The offering raised a record $81.3 billion, making it the largest IPO in history, despite growing concerns about a potential AI bubble and the technology's impact on jobs and livelihoods. Anthropic's listing could have a more direct influence on technology-focused investments because its shares are now listed on the Nasdaq. Strong demand could encourage renewed buying in AI-related stocks, although the impact may be more pronounced in technology stocks than across the broader market. Federal Reserve Rate Concerns Return Interest rate uncertainty is another factor affecting Wall Street. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC Wednesday that the central bank might need to deliver a half-percentage-point rate increase to bring persistent inflation under control. Such an increase would be larger than the quarter-point moves typically associated with the Fed's recent policy adjustments. The comments raised concerns about the possibility that borrowing costs could remain elevated or increase further. Higher interest rates can weigh on stock valuations by making bonds and other fixed-income investments more attractive relative to equities. They can also increase financing costs for businesses and households. Technology companies with valuations based heavily on expectations of future growth can be particularly sensitive to changes in interest rate expectations. The Federal Open Market Committee is scheduled to meet December 8-9. Investors were also awaiting the release of minutes from the Fed's October meeting for additional clues about policymakers' thinking. Healthcare Stocks Add Pressure to the Dow The weakness was not limited to technology companies. Healthcare stocks also weighed heavily on the Dow after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services proposed a new anti-fraud rule affecting insurance providers. The proposed Comprehensive Regulations to Uncover Suspicious Healthcare, known as the CRUSH rule, would increase audits of insurance companies and could require providers to return certain overpayments. UnitedHealth Group and Humana's shares both fell around 6 percent. Because the Dow is a price-weighted index containing 30 major companies, substantial declines in some of its largest components can have an outsized effect on its performance. The healthcare sell-off added to the pressure on the index alongside concerns about technology stocks. What Happens Next for Wall Street? The next several trading sessions could prove important for investors attempting to determine whether the recent weakness represents a temporary correction or the beginning of a more prolonged downturn. Nvidia's earnings have provided evidence that demand for AI infrastructure remains strong, but the market's reaction suggests investors are increasingly concerned about valuations, corporate leadership and the financial sustainability of the AI boom. Meanwhile, Waller's comments have introduced another source of uncertainty as traders consider the possibility of additional monetary tightening. Anthropic's successful debut demonstrated that investor demand for AI companies remains substantial, but it did little to prevent Thursday's broader market sell-off. With the Dow now below 50,000, the more important question for investors is whether the forces weighing on Wall Street begin to ease before the end of the year. The broader market will need reassurance that inflation is moderating, corporate earnings remain resilient and the Federal Reserve is not preparing to raise borrowing costs aggressively. news.summary: The Dow tumbled more than 1,100 points, falling below the milestone the former attorney general cited during her Epstein hearing.

news.title: Trump, Xi, Putin Hold Historic 3-way Summit, Pledge Peaceful Use of Nuclear Weapons
news.text:
Call for UN reforms, caution ICC against abusing its jurisdiction 

•Pledge increased production, supply of refined petroleum products

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

The leaders of the United States, China and Russia yesterday held a historic trilateral summit, with Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin pledging to prevent nuclear proliferation, reduce nuclear risks and ensure that nuclear weapons are never used in a war.

The meeting, which brought together the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers for the first time in such a format, ended with a joint declaration outlining areas of cooperation, including nuclear security, global peace, energy supply and reforms of international institutions.

At the centre of their declaration was a reaffirmation of the principle that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, against the backdrop of persistent geopolitical tensions and the growing risk of confrontation among major powers.

The three countries also committed to maintaining dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, signalling a shared recognition of the consequences of a nuclear confrontation despite their differences on several international issues.

Trump, Xi and Putin met for more than an hour at a villa surrounded by wooded hills beside a lake in Shenzhen, southern China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

Describing the gathering as a historic moment, Trump said at the beginning of the meeting: “We are really making history. The three of us have a great deal to discuss.”

The American president also defended the importance of direct engagement among global leaders, declaring that “no peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”

The meeting followed separate engagements between Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts, both of whom the US president had described as friends.

Beyond nuclear security, the joint statement contained positions on the future of global governance, particularly the United Nations and the International Criminal Court (ICC).

The three leaders called for reforms of the United Nations (UN) to enable it to respond more effectively to global challenges and fulfil its fundamental responsibility of maintaining international peace and security.

They also warned the ICC and other similar international bodies against abusing their jurisdiction, stressing the importance of state consent and respect for the immunities of government officials.

The position could further complicate relations with European Union (EU) and NATO countries, particularly as Putin faces an international arrest warrant issued by the ICC over alleged war crimes connected to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

The Trump administration has also taken a confrontational position towards the court, imposing sanctions on it. US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, had previously said Washington wanted to dismantle the ICC.

On energy, the three countries emphasised the importance of maintaining stable global supplies, pledging to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.

The commitment comes amid disruptions to international shipping and rising oil prices following the US-Israeli war against Iran, which has affected commercial movements through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.

Trump said he and Xi shared strong concerns about ensuring that oil continued to flow through the waterway, a critical passage for global energy supplies. 

Putin, meanwhile, said the three countries had numerous shared interests in resolving regional conflicts, including the war in Ukraine, which began with Russia’s invasion in February 2022.

The Russian president also highlighted Moscow’s importance to food and energy security in the Asia-Pacific region.

The trilateral meeting took place against the background of renewed efforts to manage trade tensions between Washington and Beijing, following an extension of their trade truce earlier this month.

The gathering also followed speeches by Xi and Putin at the APEC summit, where they criticised Western trade protectionism and sanctions, with the Chinese leader advocating free and open trade.
news.summary: • Call for UN reforms, caution ICC against abusing its jurisdiction  •Pledge increased production, supply of refined petroleum products Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja The leaders of the United States, China

news.title: Melania Hit With Biggest Snub at Cringe MAGA Series Premiere
news.text:
As with her documentary, the new series will air exclusively on Amazon Prime, owned by Trump-friendly billionaire Jeff Bezos.

While Melania, 56, attended the New York premiere on Thursday, her 80-year-old husband was noticeably absent. After the softball question, the reporter then asked the first lady if she was “concerned” about potential investigations into her family by Democrats after Republicans’ midterm elections drubbing.

“Well, we went through a lot already, and we are used to it,” she said.

news.title: Meta says 'reevaluating' 2030 net zero target amid AI buildout
news.text: Meta said Thursday it was reconsidering its 2030 deadline for net zero emissions because of the artificial intelligence boom, the latest in a broad retreat by corporations on global warming targets."We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones -- including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal," Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability, said in the company's annual sustainability report.The company reported its net carbon equivalent emissions increased 45 percent in 2025 to 11.8 million metric tons -- a figure that is itself based on accounting methods viewed skeptically by climate advocates."When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned. The reality has been far more complex," the executives wrote, adding that delivering on Meta's vision "requires building the infrastructure that powers AI."In 2020, Meta set a goal of net zero emissions across its entire value chain by the year 2030, in order to align with the Paris Agreement, which seeks to hold long-term warming to 1.5C to avert climate catastrophes.This involves eliminating emissions as far as possible and purchasing credits from carbon removal projects where emissions cannot be eliminated.The value chain covers emissions from sources such as purchased goods and services and capital goods -- equipment, machinery, buildings, facilities and vehiclesA study published in Nature Sustainability this week found that 403 of the United States' most powerful data centers accounted for around two percent of the country's electricity consumption and a carbon footprint comparable to Denmark -- figures that are only growing.Around 1,200 such "hyperscale" data centers are now online and hundreds more are planned.Green retreatUnder President Donald Trump's second term, major American businesses have stepped back from environmental commitments.Though the explosion of AI data centers looms large over the trend, it is not confined to Big Tech, with car makers, retailers and beverage companies also offenders.In January 2021, GM set a target of 100 percent zero-emission vehicle sales by 2035.While it technically maintains this target, the company this year backed the Trump administration's weakening of a fuel economy rule to a level that would require no further improvement.In 2020 retail giant Walmart committed to cutting emissions by around a third by 2025 and two-thirds by 2030 from a 2015 baseline. But in a 2024 report it acknowledged it would miss the first target as well as its recycling goals.Also in 2020, Google pledged to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, in what CEO Sundar Pichai heralded as a "moonshot." But by 2024 it had stopped claiming its operations were carbon neutral, and this year it acknowledged its emissions were still rising.Beverage giants Coca-Cola and Pepsi have changed the baseline years for their emissions reduction targets and weakened their ambitions.
news.summary: Meta said Thursday it was reconsidering its 2030 deadline for net zero emissions because of the artificial intelligence boom, the latest in a broad retreat by corporations on global warming targets. news.title: DOJ dropping Alaska midterms Senate certification lawsuit, saying case is 'moot'
news.text:
The Justice Department is giving up on its controversial lawsuit that sought to potentially block the certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate race, telling an appeals court Thursday evening that the issue is now "moot" in an apparent acknowledgment of Democratic Senator-elect Mary Peltola's current lead in the electoral tally. 

The Associated Press projected Tuesday that Peltola will win the race for the Senate, the ninth Senate pickup for Democrats in the next Congress.

Ahead of the election, President Donald Trump had directed the Justice Department to preemptively file a lawsuit to try to block the certification of the crucial Alaska Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan lost, citing name confusion among the candidates.

Republicans have alleged that candidate Dan J. Sullivan was running a sham campaign to purposefully confuse voters and draw votes away from incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan based on their names being similar.

A federal judge in Alaska dismissed the lawsuit on Nov. 1, saying there was "no workable plan" to investigate the claims in relation to the votes submitted.

In a Thursday filing from DOJ's third-ranked official Stanley Woodward, the department requested the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals vacate the order entered by a district judge in Alaska that dismissed DOJ's lawsuit -- but still acknowledged the dispute is now not worth any further litigation. 

"This Court should deny the motion to summarily affirm the district court’s judgment," Woodward said. "Instead, this Court should vacate the district court’s order dismissing this lawsuit, because the case has become moot."

Later in the filing, Woodward opines on what he describes as an unfair hand given to the Trump administration in being unable to dispute ballots that may have been accidentally cast for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan instead of incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

"The United States therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means of “determin[ing] whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan” and vindicating the United States’ asserted injury," Woodward writes. 

The filing comes after days of President Donald Trump repeatedly calling for the Alaska election results to be ruled in favor of Sen. Sullivan by combining the votes of Dan J. Sullivan as well as another Republican candidate he alleges was unlawfully recruited by Democrats as a spoiler in the race.
news.summary: The Justice Department is giving up on its controversial lawsuit that sought to potentially block the certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate race.

"Why should relations between nations be mysterious. Again, there is a need for open and clear and consistent communication between nations, not only for the purposes of crisis management, but for ongoing dialogs that can enhance understanding and peace," he said.

The presidents of Russia, the United States and China held a meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, the first such meeting ever. The heads of state exchanged views on the current international situation and expressed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security. news.title: Trump says no rush on Iran decision, looks to next year
news.text:
US President Donald Trump on Thursday appeared to push a decision ​on renewed major strikes against Iran into next year, extending a timeline that he had previously suggested could come to a ‌head after this month's US midterm elections.

Asked in a Reuters interview about the possibility of new strikes, Trump said: “Well, I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year.”

“We’ve got time," added Trump, speaking from his plane as he returned to Washington from his trip to China.

In recent weeks, Trump has alternated between threats of escalation against Iran ​and indicating he could wind down hostilities, with the two sides in a standoff over efforts to resolve the conflict.

Trump gave a similar timeline in ​two other interviews. "We'll see what happens after January 1," he told Fox News in an interview that aired on Thursday, ⁠while saying in a separate interview with a reporter for Axios and Israel's News 12: "I'm not rushing to make any decisions on Iran."

In the ​weeks leading up to the November 3 congressional contests, Trump repeatedly suggested that Iran would be more willing to strike a deal in the eight-month conflict ​following the US elections.

But after his fellow Republicans lost both chambers of Congress, his administration last week said it believes its blockade and economic sanctions against Iran are working. The US Senate, which Republicans control until January 3, again on Thursday rejected a measure aimed at curbing the war.

Trump has acknowledged Iran played a role in the losses but has ​said he would not have changed course.

Vice President JD Vance, a possible 2028 presidential candidate, publicly distanced himself from the war, which he blamed for ​the party's political rout. Trump later directed Vance to step back from Iran diplomatic efforts and focus on domestic matters.

"JD was fine," Trump said when Reuters asked about the vice president's social media post. "What he said was right. He said that the whole situation is one of the reasons certainly that the election didn’t go our way."

"And the big thing is if you had to do it again, would you do it? And the answer is yes. Because you can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.

Thursday's joint statement, issued after Trump's summit with his Russian and Chinese counterparts, did not mention the conflict with Iran.

DOWNPLAYS BOMB THREAT

Trump, on Fox ​News, was also asked about a ​report carried by CNN this week that ⁠Iran was planning to detonate a "dirty bomb" in Washington. A dirty bomb uses conventional explosives to spread radioactive material.

He appeared to downplay such a threat, saying, "I don't think so" when asked if people in the capital should be alarmed, ​although he also said there were indications Iran was "looking at" biological or chemical weapons, without elaborating.

"There is indication ​that Iran is looking ⁠at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear. Nuclear is much harder. And they're looking at gas and ... biological weapons — not nice — and other things," Trump said.

Iran's Foreign Ministry, in a post on X, said US accusations about Tehran developing chemical and biological weapons were intended to create fear and ⁠justify military ​action. Earlier this week, it called the CNN report "baseless."

Israel, the United States and other Western ​countries have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, which Tehran denies. Destroying Iran's nuclear programme was one of Trump's main justifications when he launched strikes against Iran in February alongside Israel.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump on Thursday appeared to push a decision ​on renewed major strikes against Iran into next year, extending a timeline that he had previously suggested could come to a ‌head after this month's US midterm elections.

news.title: Vance Roasted After Throwing Himself Into Major New Release
news.text:
He shared an AI–generated image of himself and Trump standing side by side on a mock GTA poster, surrounded by a collage of MAGA imagery.

What caught people’s attention on X, however, was Vance replacing the game’s title with “the golden age XLVII”–referring to Donald Trump, the 47th president. 

Users quickly ripped the post to shreds, with many sharply disagreeing that the U.S. is prosperous right now.

The backlash to his post was immediate. “Buddy, I’m broke as sh*t. Where is this Golden Age?” wrote one user. Another responded: “Is the golden age in the room with us right now?”

Others criticized Vance and the Republicans’ thrashing in the midterm elections, noting that “the golden age doesn’t have blue Texas, JD.” Another proclaimed: “This is why you lost the midterms.” 

Some just wanted the vice president to let them enjoy the new game. “Can you let people enjoy GTA for like 5 seconds before you have to make it all weird?” one pleaded.

Away from social media, it’s not been a very good month for the vice president in the polls, either.

A stunning new poll this week revealed that he is now trailing Secretary of State Marco Rubio by double digits as the preferred 2028 presidential candidate amongst Republican primary voters.

Rubio now has 36 percent of his party’s primary voters naming him as their favorite nominee in two years. Just 20 percent of those surveyed preferred Vance.

This time last year, Vance led Rubio by nearly 50 points—54 percent to six percent—in the same Emerson College survey.

Vance had always been seen as the most likely to inherit MAGA’s crown even as the 80-year-old president remained coy about whom he would endorse.

Now the vice president’s problem, it seems, is that he is strongly tied to Trump, with his near record-low approval ratings, a disastrous war in Iran, and voters’ massive rejection of the Republican Party and the MAGA movement as a whole.

Even Utah’s Republican governor, Spencer Cox, suggested that Vance move on from his presidential ambitions.

“It’s time for the next thing,” Cox told Politico this week.

MAGA podcaster Ben Shapiro went so far as to blame Vance for weakening the party as a whole.

“I look at Trump’s coalition, and I say, I’m not sure where Vice President Vance doesn’t shrink that coalition,” Shapiro told NPR. 

The vice president’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Daily Beast.
news.summary:
VP/XJ.D. Vance has been roasted online after trying to join the latest viral phenomenon in a late-night tweet. 

Posting from Washington, D.C., while his boss was returning from China, Vice President Vance tried to join the Grand Theft Auto VI hype, to no avail. 

Read more at The Daily Beast.

news.title: Putin-Trump contacts indicate possibility of improving ties — ex-congressman
news.text:
WASHINGTON, November 20. /TASS/. Contacts between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US leader Donald Trump in Shenzhen indicate the possibility to improve bilateral relations, former US Congressman Dennis Kucinich told TASS.

"When President Trump greeted President Putin as his friend, that was very significant because it means that there is a path towards improved relations between our countries," said Kucinich, who represented Ohio in the lower chamber of Congress from 1997 to 2013.

After the bilateral meeting, the two leaders were joined by Chinese President Xi Jinping for talks in a trilateral format.

"When you have three of the most important leaders in the world come together, just meeting, just coming together in the same place, and talking, it is so important because when leaders of nations refuse to talk to each other, it creates a gap, which can be filled, unfortunately, with misunderstandings and misinformation," added the former lawmaker, who ran for president in 2004 and 2008 and served as mayor of Cleveland, Ohio. "And so, face to face discussions should always be at a premium in international relations."

Kucinich went on to say that the final declaration, adopted by the three leaders, mentions the three countries’ plans to boost oil production and deliveries.

"The fact that there was a discussion about increasing production and supply of refined petroleum products is important in a couple different ways. First of all, with respect to Russia, the easing of any sanctions on energy is very important," he said.

The presidents of Russia, the United States and China held a meeting on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, the first such meeting ever. The heads of state exchanged views on the current international situation and expressed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security. The leaders also adopted a declaration on peace.
news.summary: Dennis Kucinich separately said that the final declaration approved at the trilateral summit, which took place after the meeting between the two leaders, mentions Russia, the US and China's plans to boost oil production and deliveries, which could lead to an easing of sanctions against Russia in the energy sector

news.title: Georgia’s New Governor-Elect Makes Her First Public Gaffe
news.text:
Georgia’s newly elected Democratic governor suffered her first political stumble after her transition website briefly listed at least two deceased figures and a prominent MAGA supporter among her advisers.

Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated billionaire Republican Rick Jackson in the Georgia governor’s race as Democrats made sweeping gains in midterm contests nationwide.

Bottoms had pledged to challenge Donald Trump, making the names initially displayed on her transition team website all the more surprising.

Vernon Jones, a former Democratic lawmaker who later became a Republican and once described himself as the “Black Donald Trump,” appeared on the list, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.

His inclusion drew attention because Jones has previously argued that civil rights protections should not be extended to LGBTQ+ people, saying they “can actually change.”

The website also named two celebrated Democrats who could not have joined the transition team because both had died.

Congressman John Lewis, the civil rights leader who took part in the Freedom Rides and the March on Washington, was listed as a team member.

Former US Senator Max Cleland was also included. Lewis died in 2020, while Cleland died the following year.

Mary Norwood, a former Atlanta City Council member who challenged Bottoms in the 2017 mayoral election, was also mistakenly named.

Bottoms’ office told the AJC that the list was posted in error, although it has not explained how the names came to appear on the website.

A former Atlanta mayor and one-time White House adviser to Joe Biden, Bottoms declared that she would be a “governor for all of Georgia” after winning by nine points.

Senator Jon Ossoff, a frequent campaign ally of Bottoms, also won his race on Tuesday night. The pair had brought former President Barack Obama into Georgia for their final campaign events.

The result represented a major setback for Trump in Georgia, a traditionally conservative Southern state that has shifted toward swing-state status in recent years.

Bottoms connected with voters by presenting herself as a native Georgian with deep roots in the region. On the campaign trail, she frequently said she was “at least a fifth-generation Georgian.”

“I say ‘at least’ because we can only trace our family back five generations to a plantation in Crawfordville,” she told audiences.

The descendant of enslaved people is now the first Democrat to head to the Georgia Governor’s Mansion in nearly three decades, making her one of the country’s most prominent newly elected Democrats.

Georgia’s results were among the most closely watched in the country, with political analysts noting that the outcome could influence the 2028 Democratic presidential primary and Ossoff’s potential national ambitions.

Many Democrats view Ossoff as a possible presidential contender. His forceful anti-Trump message, youthful profile and ability to appeal to moderate voters have all fueled speculation about a White House bid.

Although Ossoff has said he has “no interest” in running for president, skeptics have questioned whether that position will hold. Bottoms’ victory as governor could make a future campaign more attractive.

If Ossoff ran for president and won, Georgia’s governor would appoint his replacement in the Senate. With Bottoms now set to occupy that office, leaving the Senate could appear less risky to him.

The governor’s race grew increasingly combative, with Jackson and Bottoms repeatedly attacking each other’s records.

Jackson frequently criticized Bottoms’ tenure as Atlanta mayor from 2018 to 2022. His campaign advertisements featured footage of Black Lives Matter protests and unrest during the pandemic, as he accused her of “ruining” the city through soft-on-crime policies.

Bottoms rejected that portrayal, describing Jackson and Trump as out-of-touch political dinosaurs. At one event, she said it was a “long-standing playbook to paint Atlanta as this big bad place.”

Bottoms is the daughter of R&B singer Major Lance, who recorded several major hits in the 1960s, including “The Monkey Time.”

Her husband, Derek Bottoms, is an attorney and serves as The Home Depot’s vice president of employment practices and associate relations.

Bottoms began her career as a prosecutor and magistrate judge in Atlanta before making an unsuccessful 2008 bid for a seat on the Fulton County Superior Court.

Later that year, she won election to the Atlanta City Council, where she served until becoming mayor in 2017.

Her time as Atlanta’s 60th mayor was turbulent. Bottoms faced criticism over several issues, including her handling of Black Lives Matter protests and unrest during the pandemic.

Violent crime and homicides rose substantially during her tenure, with the number of murders increasing by 59 percent between 2019 and 2021.

Jackson repeatedly portrayed Bottoms as a failed mayor who left Atlanta in flames. “When the city needed her, she let Atlanta burn,” he told crowds.

Bottoms nevertheless won the gubernatorial election by more than 300,000 votes. Jackson conceded Tuesday night, saying: “Tonight, the voters spoke… And I respect their decision.”

news.title: Trump discusses nuclear risks with Putin, Xi; Kim meeting 'at some point'
news.text: Hyderabad: US President Donald Trump discussed nuclear risks and arms reduction with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping during a historic trilateral meeting during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China, but left without meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, whose country has continued to expand its nuclear weapons capabilities.Despite earlier suggestions that he could meet Kim during his Asia visit, Trump returned to Washington without holding talks with the North Korean leader. However, he indicated that a meeting could still take place in the future, saying it would happen "at some point" without providing a specific timeline."The relationship is there, but we didn't meet," Trump told NBC News on Thursday. Explaining why the meeting did not happen, he said there had been "too many meetings" and that an engagement with Kim would not have worked out during the visit..The remarks came after Trump, Putin and Xi held an unprecedented three-way meeting on the sidelines of APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. The discussions included nuclear risks, non-proliferation, the Ukraine war and the conflict involving Iran.In a joint declaration following the meeting, the three leaders agreed to hold dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons. They also reiterated that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.However, the declaration made no specific mention of North Korea or its nuclear programme, despite the country being an important part of the wider nuclear security concerns in the region. According to reports, Chinese state news agency Xinhua said the Korean Peninsula situation was among the issues discussed during the trilateral meeting..Trump had earlier indicated possibility of Kim meeting.Speculation about a possible Trump-Kim meeting had grown after the US president suggested that the North Korean leader could join him during his China visit.Speaking to reporters before departing for Asia, Trump had said, "We may meet with Kim Jong-un also, so that'll be good." He had also suggested that Kim's possible visit would depend on Chinese President Xi Jinping.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had also indicated that the Trump administration was serious about engaging with North Korea, saying dialogue was necessary to address the issues between Washington and Pyongyang..Trump and Kim last met in June 2019 at the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea. The two leaders had held three face-to-face meetings during Trump's first presidential term, but their diplomatic efforts failed to produce an agreement on North Korea's nuclear programme.While Trump has now indicated that another meeting remains possible, his latest remarks offer little clarity on when such an engagement could take place.(With inputs from agencies)

news.title: ‘Everyone is a friend’: Trump’s Asia meetings reveal contrasting approaches to world order
news.text: Washington US President Donald Trump huddled with leaders from longtime partners Japan, Australia and India in a resort conference room in Manila, Philippines, this week to strengthen a partnership called the Quad that is meant to counter China. Two days later, Trump warmly greeted Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in an unprecedented, trilateral summit of countries that have been long considered rivals to take on "new opportunities and approaches on a range of very important issues". Trump effusively described all these leaders as friends, but the meetings highlighted some key differences. The two geopolitical gatherings on the same whirlwind Asia trip reflect the US president's varied foreign policy approaches at a time when the world order is shifting. "The Quad, comprising four democracies that uphold the rule of law, represents the post-World War II international order," said Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow focused on Asia at the Hudson Institute. "The trilateral, meanwhile, raises the prospect of a very different order -- one in which three great powers stand above the rest, recognise each other's spheres of influence and refrain from interfering in each other's core interests." The Quad meeting was a much different scene than Trump-Xi-Putin summit In a no-frills hotel conference room in the Philippine capital on Tuesday, Trump sat down with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Covered in blue cloth, four long tables formed the appropriate shape of a quadrilateral, with each government taking one side. The leaders were flanked by their Cabinet members. There were no decorations but a mandatory display of national flags. Before the meeting, the four leaders took a photo together, where Trump took questions from reporters and joked around with his counterparts. Calling the leaders "friends of mine", Trump turned to Albanese and patted him on the back, as the Australian premier nodded. Trump then threw his thumb towards Modi and joked, "And by the way, he's a very tough man," before pointing to Takaichi and saying, "and she may be even tougher". Modi didn't crack a smile, but Takaichi chuckled. Trump turned back to Albanese: "And we? We're OK, too," to which the Australian laughed. Moments earlier, Modi, apparently impatient, gestured to end the press conference to no avail as Trump kept taking questions. The scene was much grander but far less spontaneous two days later when Trump joined Putin and Xi at a massive ring-shaped table with a burst of pink flowers in the middle at a state-owned resort in Shenzhen, China. The room was spacious with marble flooring, crystal chandeliers and jade sculptures. Three leaders were alone at the table, seated some distance from one another. Xi read from a prepared script, with hardly any expression on his face. Putin looked at the documents in front of him, while Trump sat back with a slight smile on the opposite end of the table. Trump says he's friends with everyone In Manila, Trump said at the Quad meeting that "we're all friends" and suggested that the leaders from Japan, Australia and India can reach him directly. "We talk a lot when they have a problem, when they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open and the Oval Office is always open to you," Trump said. Talking to reporters, Trump praised his fellow Quad leaders, calling them "phenomenal people". "And they're friends of mine, so that helps," the US president said. On Thursday, Trump described Xi and Putin similarly, addressing both as his "friend". At the airport in Shenzhen, Trump got a rare greeting there from Xi and even an unusual hug from the Chinese leader. At a welcoming ceremony for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation grouping, Putin joined Xi and Trump on stage. He and Trump shook hands and held each other briefly by the arm, with Xi looking on and smiling. At the trilateral meeting, Trump argued that differences among countries should not forestall talks. "Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And, uh, we feel the opposite," Trump said. The statements from the two meetings diverge The joint press release from the Quad leaders called the group "a force for good and a partnership of action, committed to peace, stability, and prosperity" and laid out areas for cooperation, including artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and maritime surveillance. The Chinese, US and Russian governments issued a statement committing to reforming the United Nations, planning to increase petroleum supplies and affirming opposition to nuclear wars. While the Quad statement was substantive and reflective of the alignment of the four nations, the trilateral statement was largely symbolic. Still, it offered more detail than expected, said Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia. With language about nuclear weapons and future dialogue, "it is a major concession by China," said Kagan, now a senior advisor at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
news.summary: The US President’s whirlwind Asia trip brought together rival geopolitical groupings, raising questions about Washington’s evolving approach to global power equations

news.title: Trump says nuclear arms limits with China, Russia will be very hard to achieve
news.text:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Thursday after ​talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin ‌that a mutual agreement to limit nuclear weapons will be hard to achieve but that he will keep working on it.

“I love the concept of it but ​in terms of pure negotiation, it’s a very hard thing for ​me as a president to do,” Trump told Reuters by ⁠phone as he flew back to Washington from his trilateral summit in ​China.

A top priority for Trump on the trip was to begin three-way ​talks on nuclear arms control, a topic China is reluctant to address as it mounts a large nuclear buildup to catch up with Russian and American dominance.

The Bulletin of the ​Atomic Scientists estimated China had roughly 410 nuclear warheads in 2023, compared ​with about 3,708 in the United States, according to a separate report.

A later Bulletin ‌estimate ⁠put Russia’s arsenal, the world’s largest, at about 5,420 warheads as of March 2026.

China has been rapidly expanding its arsenal, with the Pentagon projecting more than 1,000 operational warheads by 2030.

Trump said on Thursday that Xi agrees ​with him on the ​concept of limiting ⁠nuclear weapons “but at the same time it’s very hard for somebody to say ‘We have 4,000 nuclear weapons, we’ll ​give up half.’ It’s hard to do.“

He said he ​would keep ⁠bringing up the subject “because it should be done, but it’s hard to do psychologically.”

A joint statement after the talks said that the leaders “reaffirmed that a nuclear ⁠war cannot ​be won and must never be fought” ​and that they would “conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation of nuclear ​weapons.”
