news.title: APEC live: How events in Shenzhen unfolded
news.text:
SHENZHEN -- Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted leaders including U.S. counterpart Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin at this year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, showcasing his own country's technological prowess against a backdrop of cold and hot conflicts.

The proceedings in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen kicked off Tuesday with a CEO Summit of business leaders, followed by an Economic Leaders' Meeting that wrapped up on Thursday.

On the sidelines, Xi and Trump had their third summit of the year as they sought to manage a fraught superpower rivalry. The biggest moment was a historic trilateral summit among Xi, Trump and Putin, where they discussed nuclear arms and other issues.

Nikkei Asia was on the ground to cover proceedings. Here are some of the highlights:

Here's how it unfolded (Shenzhen time):

Thursday, Nov. 19

10:47 p.m. The APEC leaders' "Shenzhen Outlook" statement is still missing from the official website. However, China's state news agency Xinhua has published the statement on its news site, with the Chinese version released at 9:18 p.m. and the English one at 9:50 p.m.

"The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting adopted 2026 APEC Leaders' Shenzhen Outlook on Thursday," according to the Xinhua readout.

Shortly after, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi appeared on stage for a news conference.

The APEC secretariat did not respond to a request for comment.

8:30 p.m. Stan Shih, founder of computer maker Acer and Taiwan's representative at the APEC summit, told reporters upon returning to Taipei that he reiterated that the technology-oriented island democracy was an "indispensable partner in the progress of global AI."

After reading out his prepared remarks at Taoyuan International Airport, the tech veteran offered some personal thoughts on his trip to Shenzhen.

"I am extremely not used to it," he said, referring to having to stick to a script. "Being a political leader is so unfree," he said. "I wasn't nervous but I was definitely under pressure."

7:58 p.m. The joint statement by APEC leaders released earlier has been taken down from the official website. Originally published as the "Shenzhen Outlook," the online site shows only "404" now, indicating that the page was not found.

Nikkei Asia is reaching out to the APEC secretariat for comment.

6:55 p.m. A statement has been published from the trilateral between Trump, Xi and Putin.

China, the U.S. and Russia will increase the production and supply of oil, and the countries promised to engage in talks that would reduce nuclear risk and prevent nuclear proliferation, according to a joint statement released by China's state news agency Xinhua.

The statement, published after more than 90 minutes of discussions between the three head of states, listed four points in total. It also said the three countries would push to reform the United Nations to "more effectively address global challenges" and separately warned against overreach by the International Criminal Court.

6:45 p.m. The joint statements from APEC leaders are usually titled declarations. The one produced in Shenzhen, however, is called the "Shenzhen Outlook."

The statement affirmed the importance of efforts to "improve the trade and investment environment." However, it has no mention of the World Trade Organization or support for the multilateral trading system.

The statement encourages "voluntary exchange of good practices" to support innovation, in a nod to the AI rivalry between the U.S. and China. It also flags risks of data breaches and other use of technologies for malicious purposes.

On trade, the statement notes the importance of maintain the flow of energy and "other essential goods." It does not mention rare earths -- a key point of tension between the U.S. and China.

6:23 p.m. Putin has left the venue without making media statements, TASS reports.

6:01 p.m. The trilateral has concluded, CCTV reports. The meeting lasted more than one hour.

5:56 p.m. As we await the outcome of the trilateral meeting, here's our take on Takaichi's visit to Shenzhen.

4:50 p.m. Trump said the three countries are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons and to lessen the risk.

Trump said its not an easy thing to give up nuclear weapons, but that it is vital to work together to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries, naming Iran.

4:41 p.m. Xi described the historic meeting with Putin and Trump at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen as "groundbreaking," according to CCTV.

Xi said that "positive interaction" between major powers is mandatory and that major powers bear special responsibilities. He added that China has advanced its partnership with Russia "for a new era" and is building a "constructive and strategically stable relationship" with the U.S.

Xi also said that China, Russia and the U.S. should set an example by "cooperating to address global challenges, jointly safeguarding world peace and stability", according to CCTV.

Putin said that Russia, China and the U.S. can contribute to strengthening global stability if they cooperate constructively, according to TASS agency

4:21 p.m. According to the Chinese government's readout for the Xi-Trump bilateral, Xi said the China-U.S. relationship is stable and trending positively and hoped to continue to steer ties on the "right trajectory" with Trump.

Xi said that communication between the two countries must continue to keep pace and that both sides should expand the list of areas for cooperation while narrowing the list of problems.

On Taiwan, Xi urged the U.S. should "do the right thing to avoid major setbacks" in the bilateral relationship.

Xi said that AI should remain under human control and enhance communication and coordination to address AI security risks.

The two countries agreed to develop an "action plan" for the relationship of "constructive strategic stability," according to Xinhua.

The Chinese readout made no mention of any details to extend the trade truce, which is set to expire in January 10 2027

4:16 p.m. The Xi-Putin-Trump trilateral finally gets underway, an hour or so later than scheduled.

3:42 p.m. China's Ministry of Commerce said in a press conference that it will have an agricultural working group meeting with the U.S. "in the near future." Trump said earlier he would ask China to do more for American farmers.

3:03 p.m. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters that the country will communicate with China on common challenges. The remarks came after she met Chinese President Xi Jinping for the first time since her comments on Taiwan last November sparked a diplomatic freeze.

Takaichi said Japan's position on Taiwan remains the same.

The prime minister also said she is closely following the U.S.-China bilateral meeting. She expressed confidence that Japanese interests would not be harmed.

2:57 p.m. The Trump-Xi bilateral summit has ended, CCTV says.

2:49 p.m. Meanwhile, Taiwan's defence ministry said that two Russian military Tu-95 aircraft flew to the island's east on Thursday after approaching from the south, and then exited to its northeast.

2:10 p.m. The Kremlin said the issue of Ukraine was the main topic at the Trump-Putin bilateral, Reuters reported, citing Russia's Tass news agency.

Trump had said that he plans discuss ending the Ukraine war with Xi, and later with Xi and Putin in the bilateral.

2:06 p.m. Xi described China-U.S. relations as overall stable and improving and added he was willing to work with Trump to continue steering bilateral ties on the correct course.

"I remain committed to working with you," Xi said to Trump.

Trump also said he planned to discuss ending Ukraine war with Xi and Putin in the trilateral.

1:58 p.m. Trump said at the start of his bilateral meeting with Xi that the U.S.-China Board of Trade has brought balance to the relationship between the two countries and that they have split up tariffs in fair ways.

Trump added that he and Xi felt strongly that oil should flow through the Strait of Hormuz, where an Iranian blockade in response to U.S.-Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic has restricted shipments and pushed up energy prices. The U.S. president said he will ask China to do more for American farmers, staunch supporters of the Republican party.

1:40 p.m. Trump and Xi pose in front of U.S. and Chinese flags for photos

1:30 p.m. Trump has arrived at the Kylin Villa, a lakeside resort in Shenzhen that will serve as the venue for his bilateral summit with Xi and the trilateral including Putin.

12:43 p.m. Trump met with Putin on the sidelines of the APEC forum following the plenary leaders session. Their meeting comes ahead a bilateral between Trump and Xi and a trilateral among the three leaders.

"We've had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they'll come out of this," Trump told Putin.

1:30 p.m. Trump has arrived at the Kylin Villa, a lakeside resort in Shenzhen that will serve as the venue for his bilateral summit with Xi and the trilateral including Putin.

12:35 p.m. Elon Musk told an APEC organizer that he was a "super fan" of China, according to a social media post by Yuyuan Tiantian, an account affiliated with Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.

According to the post, the Tesla and SpaceX boss told Ren Hongbin, president of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, about his admiration for China's "magnificent buildings and natural landscapes" as well as its railway system.

Tesla will continue to increase production in China, Musk said, according to the post. He was photographed sitting in a room across Ren, wearing a black jacket, pants and shoes.

12:06 p.m. APEC plenary session ends

10:58 a.m. Putin tells his APEC counterparts that Russia contributes to regional energy security and that they can "always count on Moscow." He also invites all regional partners to use Russian logistics infrastructure.

10:39 a.m. Trump spoke about the U.S. economy and claimed his administration is taming inflation. He also said in his remarks that trade deals were forthcoming.

"The United States has been a Pacific power for hundreds of years, and we continue to work to promote growth and stability, sovereignty, prosperity, and peace throughout this region," he said.

Trump also said AI regulation needed to be carefully managed and opposed measures that would "stifle" the industry. "We won't allow that to happen," he said.

Trump said he looked forward to meeting with Xi and Putin later this afternoon. but did not elaborate. The trilateral will follow a two-way meeting between Xi and Trump, their third this year.

10:30 a.m. Putin is taking the opportunity presented by APEC to shore up ties with Asian partners. He and Vietnamese leader To Lam agreed to step up cooperation with "a focus on traditional and new energy, including nuclear power, wind power and gas-fired power," according to Vietnam's readout.

The statement also says they "underscored the importance of maintaining peace, security and stability, increasing dialogue and cooperation, and upholding the role of multilateralism, the United Nations and the fundamental principles of international law."

10:10 a.m. In his opening address, Xi called for cooperation on Al and supply chains. The Chinese president proposed building "four key pillars" for development in the Asia-Pacific: economy and trade, connectivity, innovation and development.

He said China will provide $20 million to support cooperation in areas such as digital technology and clean energy.

9:50 a.m. Xi has opened the leaders summit, with the visiting dignitaries gathered around circular tables in a large conference room under chandeliers. Moments before sitting down for the plenary session, they took a photo with Xi in the center, flanked by Putin and Trump. Takaichi was positioned in the back row to the side.

9:40 a.m. In an interview with Fox News, Trump said he spoke with Xi about artificial intelligence, and former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang only came up "briefly," Reuters reports.

"I haven't heard that she was a spy," Trump said, in reference to Huang's extramarital affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang.

9:30 a.m. APEC leaders are gathering for the forum's main event, which begins with a "family photo" before they convene for the plenary session. Xi has urged his guests to pursue "concrete results" promoting economic openness and innovation, but time is limited. Attention in the afternoon will turn to the U.S.-China bilateral meeting and the highly anticipated Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral. There are reports that Trump will squeeze in a one-on-one meeting with Putin as well, although it is unclear how substantial that would be.

9:28 a.m. While we await today's events, here's some reading. A report to U.S. Congress on Wednesday by the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission said that the unusually active" level of engagement between Trump and Xi is masking Beijing's ongoing efforts to outcompete America economically, technologically and militarily.

8:00 a.m. The most anticipated day of the APEC gathering is about to unfold. Looking at Trump's schedule, he will attend an APEC Leaders' Plenary Session at 09:45 a.m., followed by a bilateral with Xi and then a trilateral with Xi and Putin. We will also be looking out for other meetings on the sidelines. The wild card could be the arrival of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, but as always information out of the Hermit Kingdom is spotty.

12:10 a.m. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin for about 30 minutes on the sidelines of the APEC summit and related meetings in Shenzhen, their countries' first face-to-face leaders' meeting since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022.

According to the Japanese government's account of the talks, Takaichi pressed Putin to release a Japanese journalist detained for more than a month and reverse measures putting Japan Tobacco's Russian subsidiaries under local management. The two agreed to maintain communication at various levels.

Wednesday, Nov. 18

9:20 p.m. In a welcome speech at the banquet, Xi called on APEC leaders to work toward "concrete results" when they convene Thursday morning. He said they will discuss expanding mutual openness, explore paths for innovation-driven growth and broaden opportunities for practical cooperation across various sectors, state news agency Xinhua reports.

Xi said that since his first visit to Shenzhen in 1978, the small fishing village has become a "gateway for China's high-standard opening-up."

"Openness is in Shenzhen's DNA," he is quoted as saying.

9:00 p.m. Footage and photos coming out of the APEC leaders' banquet show some highly anticipated diplomatic interactions. Trump and Putin are seen shaking hands as Xi looks on, a prelude to Thursday's closely watched trilateral summit.

Xi also is pictured shaking hands with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. This was a major "will they or won't they" question ahead of the summit, as China-Japan ties have been frosty for over a year, since Takaichi spoke about a potential Taiwan crisis in the Japanese parliament. Takaichi is pictured smiling broadly at Xi after the greeting.

7:00 p.m. Chinese leader Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, are hosting a banquet at the Shenzhen International Exchange Center for APEC leaders. Live footage from state broadcaster CCTV shows U.S. President Donald Trump arriving at the venue.

6:00 p.m. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung held talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping earlier amid speculation that Trump could meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Shenzhen.

Xi told Lee he is willing to support "various efforts aimed at easing tensions on the Korean Peninsula, including a North Korea-U.S. dialogue," according to South Korean National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac, as quoted by the Yonhap news agency.

Lee had asked China to play "a constructive role" in addressing Korean Peninsula issues, which the South Korean president described as a "do or die" matter, according to the same Yonhap report.

Chinese state-owned news outlet Xinhua made no mention of a potential Trump-Kim summit or of Korean Peninsula tensions in its account of the meeting published Wednesday afternoon.

Xi and Lee acknowledged that next year marks the 35th anniversary of their countries' diplomatic relations. Xinhua said Xi called the anniversary an opportunity to promote the steady development of their ties. Xi also mentioned that both countries are "beneficiaries of multilateralism and free trade," poking at a possible wedge between the U.S. and its key Asian ally, given Trump's tariff policies.

Lee called for strengthening the neighbors' relations "based on the mutual trust and friendship the two countries have built so far," referring to the anniversary, according to Yonhap.

5:05 p.m. Xi greets Trump on the tarmac, reciprocating a rare airport welcome that Trump afforded him when he visited Washington in September. Ties between the rival superpowers have grown increasingly tense in recent weeks over tech restrictions and other contentious points, but the Shenzhen gathering provides the two leaders an opportunity to maintain their fragile trade truce. At the airport, the atmosphere appears friendly, with the presidents chatting and smiling before making their way past an honor guard and a welcome crew waving Chinese and American flags.

Xi stands and waves as Trump departs in his black limo, known as the Beast.

4:45 p.m. Trump lands in Shenzhen. TV footage shows Air Force One taxiing at the airport.

3:30 p.m. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese reveals in remarks to CEOs that he spoke with Xi about his first visit to Shenzhen back in 1998, when he was a young politician. Back then, the city was still a long way away from becoming the tech hub it is today.

"You don't think of it as a same place," he said. Like Thailand's Anutin immediately before him, Albanese called Shenzhen an example of the region's success.

3:00 p.m. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul recounts how Chinese Premier Li Qiang "kept telling me the story of Shenzhen" when they met in Bangkok on Friday, about how a fishing village four decades ago became a global business metropolis.

Anutin said he interpreted the story of the APEC host city as an example of how a "transformation can be achieved where an economy opens itself up."

The Thai leader touted the benefits of Thailand's preparations to join the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development. "Our OECD accession process is helping improve governance and regulatory standards and transparency," he said.

Regarding online scam groups that are active especially in Thailand's border regions with Myanmar and Cambodia, Anutin stresses that there is a "global partnership" to fight cross-border organized crime.

2:15 p.m. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney tells APEC's business gathering that his country is taking "practical steps" with China on financial cooperation, including for times of stress. He also cites growing collaboration in the green economy sector, crediting China's wind and solar industries for the opportunities they create.

Carney -- whose government has faced friction with the U.S. under Trump despite the neighbors' traditionally tight ties -- has made a point this year to improve relations with China.

Praising the Chinese leadership that turned Shenzhen into a tech hub, he said, "The choices that built this city will lift this whole region." And he says that "Canada has made our choice to build a more stronger, prosperous and a more sovereign future."

Carney alluded to geopolitical tensions, saying "it's no insight to say that this has been a difficult year for international consensus." However, he said, APEC is delivering on tangible cooperation.

12:00 p.m. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung meets with Xi on the sidelines, and tells him that he wants to work together to promote peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula, according to the media pool. Xi tells his guest that he is willing to work with South Korea on preserving stable industrial supply chains.

Their meeting comes amid growing rumblings that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un could make an appearance at APEC to meet with some attendees, including Trump. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters earlier in Manila that Trump is "serious" about engaging with Kim and "prepared to do it," although he acknowledged that a meeting might not materialize.

11:30 a.m. Russian President Vladimir Putin piles on with implicit criticism of the U.S., saying that "former dominant powers" have tried to suppress the development of other countries.

"Economic domination and coercion are now a thing of the past," he says, praising nations that have preserved their own identities and independence and arguing that sanctions and tariffs have not held Russia back.

He hails Shenzhen as a "modern vibrant megacity" and a symbol of tech, economic and social transformation in China and Asia. The region, he says, is setting an example of a "more fair, democratic and equal world order."

Putin also says he expects significant benefits from his upcoming trilateral meeting with Xi and Trump.

11:15 a.m. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is the next to address business leaders after China's Xi. While praising the host several times, Anwar delivers thinly veiled criticism of the U.S., without naming it directly. He stresses the importance of free and open business activity, emphasizing, "You can't say in one voice [that you're] promoting trade and investment, but only to your country."

11:10 a.m. Stan Shih, the founder of computer maker Acer and Taiwan's representative to the APEC summit, says he will "actively" engage with other members in Shenzhen as he departs from Taipei, according to Reuters.

APEC is one of the few international organizations that includes Taiwan, which participates as "Chinese Taipei." The administration is sending Shih in lieu of President Lai Ching-te, who Beijing considers a "separatist" because he rejects its territorial claim to Taiwan.

Shih describes Taiwan as a "trustworthy" player in the region and an indispensable partner for the global technology and AI sectors. He vows to "show the international community Taiwan's strength and contributions."

"Taiwan will go with a smile," he says.

10:10 a.m. Xi addresses the APEC CEO Summit, his first time to do so in person since 2018 in Papua New Guinea. Positioning himself as an advocate for stability, he called for resolving differences through dialogue and for defending free and open trade. He is discussing the dilemmas economies face between being open or closed, between cooperation and division and between change or taking a conservative approach. "These are all questions of our time that we must answer," he said.

9:45 a.m. The second day of APEC proceedings is about to get underway. Putin landed in Shenzhen overnight, while Trump is expected to fly in later in the day, as is Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. A number of leaders, including Xi and Putin, are due to deliver speeches to business participants, with more bilateral mettings on the sidelines.

Tuesday, Nov. 17

5:30 p.m. Xi continues his day of meetings with visiting leaders, sitting down separately with Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum, Peru's Keiko Fujimori and Chile's Jose Antonio Kast.

Mexico last year riled China by approving higher tariffs on countries with which it does not have trade deals, affecting hundreds of products. The move was widely seen as an effort to close a "back door" to the U.S.

Sheinbaum told Xi she is eager to step up cooperation with China in areas related to technology, agriculture, water, health and tourism, according to Reuters.

4:30 p.m. Speculation that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un could appear at APEC and meet with Trump continues to grow. Russia's Interfax news agency has cited the Kremlin as saying that Putin could also meet Kim if he shows up in Shenzhen, adding weight to the prospect of a Kim visit.

Shortly before he departed the U.S. for Asia, Trump himself suggested that a meeting with Kim could happen. Trump met Kim three times during his first presidency and has expressed interest in a reunion.

3:30 p.m. BYD Chairman and President Wang Chuanfu says on a panel that the electric carmaker's Thailand and Indonesia plants have created 6,000 local jobs each and nearly all of its employees at the factories are local hires.

"Our goal is not merely to export Chinese technology globally; we also aim to generate local employment and tax revenue, fostering mutually beneficial cooperation and win-win outcomes," he said.

Wang added that its Thailand factory sources just over half of components domestically.

His comments come as a rush of Chinese vehicle exports stokes trade tensions with some partner economies.

2:00 p.m. Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape has assured Xi that Taiwan no longer operates in his country. PNG pushed for the closure of Taipei's representative office in its capital, Port Moresby, and Taiwan announced earlier this month that it would indeed shut down the mission.

Marape told Xi that he hopes the move "assists you in your efforts for reunification," referring to China's claim to Taiwan, which the administration in Taipei rejects.

Taiwan had been a major buyer of gas from PNG, but said it would halt spot purchases in reaction to the closure. China, in turn, committed to increasing its purchases.

12:30 p.m. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said there is now "greater predictability and stability" in his country's ties with China, as he met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. Xi said that since the two leaders agreed to promote a strategic partnership back in January, exchanges and cooperation between China and Canada have fully resumed.

Carney's visit to Beijing in January thawed a relationship that had been severely strained in recent years, especially after the 2018 detention of Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada and the subsequent jailing of two Canadians on espionage charges -- all of whom were eventually released.

A statement released by Carney's office about Tuesday's meeting says that Canada "has recalibrated our relationship with China -- strategically, pragmatically, and decisively." It also says the two sides agreed to extend and expand a preliminary agreement to address trade issues, opening up greater access to the Chinese market for Canada's farmers and seafood harvesters and securing more tariff relief for about 400 million Canadian dollars ($280 million) worth of exports.

The statement also mentions a slew of other initiatives to boost trade, e-commerce, educational exchanges and air travel.

11:30 a.m. Trump's Air Force One made a refueling stop in Alaska before a layover in the Philippines, where Manila is hosting ASEAN leaders and related summits.

Before leaving Washington, Trump said he might meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China. The hermit nation is not a member of APEC and South Korean officials played down the possibility of such a meeting, Yonhap News Agency reported on Nov. 11.

Trump's planned attendance at APEC contrasts with last year's summit in Gyeongju, South Korea, when he met Xi Jinping in Busan and secured a trade truce but left before the main agenda began. His Shenzhen engagement signals an effort to keep ties with Xi on track ahead of next month's G20 Summit in Miami, where they are expected to meet again.

9:30 a.m. Beijing has yet to formally respond to Washington's latest move to tighten China's access to advanced artificial intelligence chips through overseas data centers. Vice Premier He Lifeng raised concerns over U.S. restrictions on China in a phone call earlier this month.

The broader AI boom is also rattling markets. Shenzhen's tech-heavy ChiNext Index sank 4.4% on Monday to a nearly 16-month low, led by steep losses among suppliers to AI data centers. U.S. stocks also fell sharply ahead of Nvidia's earnings on Tuesday.

9:00 a.m. Foreign leaders are trickling into Shenzhen. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape arrived on Monday, according to Chinese media.

The leaders are expected to hold bilateral meetings with Xi on Tuesday, according to media reports. Carney is visiting China for the second time this year. In January, he met with Xi and lowered Canada's tariff wall on Chinese electric vehicles by setting up an import quota. Among the topics expected to be discussed during his visit to Shenzhen is Chinese investment into Canada's auto sector.

Trade tensions loom over Sheinbaum's visit, after she raised import tariffs on cars, textiles, appliances and other items from countries without free trade agreements with Mexico, including China. In addition to meeting Xi, she is expected to speak at the CEO Summit on Tuesday.

news.title: Senate passes bill simplifying permitting rules to build in America, sending it to House
news.text: WASHINGTON — The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday night to pass a sweeping bill to simplify and overhaul permitting rules for energy and infrastructure projects. The bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, was crafted by an unusual coalition of Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va.; Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I.; Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. The legislation would revise and speed up environmental reviews with tighter deadlines; accelerate electricity transmission; restrict the power of federal agencies to revoke existing permits; and reduce chokepoints for approving and completing projects. To conservatives, it’s about cutting government bureaucracy. “For far too long, critical investments in our nation’s infrastructure, energy production, and economy have been forced to sit on the sidelines due to endless red tape, duplicative reviews, and regulatory uncertainty,” Capito said. For liberals, it’s an opportunity to make it easier to build long-sought projects, including clean energy, and address high costs. “Democrats are focused on lowering energy costs, reducing emissions, and stopping data centers’ free ride,” Whitehouse said. “Americans will start to get some relief quickly if this bill passes.” In an attempt to alleviate Americans’ concerns about data centers, the bill would require “new data centers of 20 megawatts or more to pay the full incremental cost of the infrastructure built to serve them,” according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. The legislation sparked opposition from some environmental groups and Native American tribal organizations, which objected to easing reviews and consultation rules that can be used to protect their interests. The bulk of the opposition in the Senate came from Democrats. Still, the willingness to simplify permitting rules represents a philosophical shift for the Democrats who endorsed it. Part of the reason is that liberal policy experts recognized that existing laws hinder their own goals. “This removes a lot of the obstacles that hamstrung [Joe] Biden’s climate investments,” said Adam Jentleson, a former Senate Democratic aide and founder of the research group Searchlight Institute. “A big part of the Inflation Reduction Act — a lot of the projects couldn’t break ground because of all the red tape.” The bill still needs approval from the House, where Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., expressed optimism that Congress will send a bill to President Donald Trump’s desk. “Well, we want to see a bill pass both chambers,” Scalise said when asked if the House will take up the Senate version of the legislation. “Obviously, the details matter. ... Hopefully, they pass a good bill back, and if not, we’ll work out those differences. But we want to get a bill to the president’s desk, and that’s still got a great chance to happen.” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said the clearest path to making a law is for the House to take the Senate’s measure and pass it, noting that it has been through extensive debate. “It has been litigated now for months. Continues to be,” Thune told reporters. “Everything gets more complicated over here procedurally, and if it were to go over there and then come back over here, I can’t predict what happens. So hopefully there’ll be the critical mass there to move it. ... It’s been through the full monty when it comes to the legislating process.”
news.summary: The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday night to pass a sweeping bill to simplify and overhaul permitting rules for energy and infrastructure projects.
news.author: Sahil Kapur

news.title: Ravens Sideline Marlon Humphrey for Saying Baltimore Best at 'Making Criminals'
news.text:
Baltimore Ravens Head Coach Jesse Minter said Thursday that cornerback Marlon Humphrey has been sent home and will miss Sunday’s game with the Carolina Panthers, after the 10-year veteran said on his podcast that the city is “best at making criminals.”

Minter said the deactivation covers a single game. Humphrey, who has started all 10 games this season, will not practice this week.

The coach told reporters the decision was reached inside the building.

“Internal conversations, obviously with myself and the leadership of the organization, we’ve decided to deactivate Marlon for this game, this upcoming week,” Minter said.

The remark came on the most recent episode of The Marlon Humphrey Show. Asked what Baltimore is best at making, Humphrey first offered The Star-Spangled Banner and National Bohemian beer. Then came the line that got clipped and passed around social media.

“They’re best at making criminals,” he said. “Yeah, no, that’s obviously going to get cut out.”

The episode is no longer posted on his YouTube page.

Humphrey apologized Wednesday in the Ravens’ open locker room, a day before the team acted.

“I’ve been here my whole career, I’ve spent lots of offseasons here, welcomed a son here,” the four-time Pro Bowl selection said. “I’m an investor in the city, investor in various parts of the state. Obviously, I do know the effect that words have, and I just like to apologize for those comments.”

Democrat Mayor Brandon Scott argued the apology fell short.

“While we acknowledge Marlon’s apology, a verbal apology is not enough,” Scott said in a statement posted to social media, calling Baltimore “a city full of young Black boys who look to the Ravens as a beacon of light in their lives.”

The mayor then turned to Humphrey’s own position, insisting he wondered how the player would feel if prominent Baltimoreans implied the city “once produced great defensive backs but we have recently lost our way.” He invited the cornerback to sit down with him and Baltimoreans who have re-entered the community.

Minter described the player as contrite.

“He’s very remorseful. I think he really understands that words mean a lot, especially to people in this city,” the Ravens coach said.

Baltimore’s crime rate has drawn repeated criticism from Republicans. President Donald Trump called the city “out of control, crime-ridden” in an August 2025 post on Truth Social and said he would send in the National Guard if the city needed help.

Minter declined to say what Humphrey must do to return for Week 12 against Houston.

Not everyone on X sided with the mayor. Users replying to the New York Post’s post about the remark said the cornerback had the city pegged.
news.summary:
Baltimore Ravens Head Coach Jesse Minter said Thursday that cornerback Marlon Humphrey has been sent home and will miss Sunday’s game with the Carolina Panthers, after the 10-year veteran said on his podcast that the city is “best at making criminals.”

news.title: Justice Department moves to end Alaska suit after Mary Peltola wins 50.13%
news.text:
The Justice Department asked a federal appeals court Thursday to declare its effort to block certification of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race moot, pointing to Democrat Mary Peltola’s victory two days earlier.

The department had sued before the midterms to prevent certification unless Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan won. Its challenge focused on another candidate with the same name, Dan J. Sullivan, who taught school before retiring in the fishing community of Petersburg.

Peltola received 50.13% of the vote, enough for an outright majority and more than the three other candidates combined, so no ranked-choice count was needed. The votes for either Sullivan consequently did not alter the result, as NBC News noted.

The department said the second Sullivan’s ballots are now mixed with the others. “The United States therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means of determin[ing] whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan,” its attorneys wrote.

Federal attorneys asked the 9th Circuit to vacate the lower court’s dismissal order, which would erase the ruling. They wrote that the suit “was always to make sure that voters had the opportunity to cast a vote accurately reflecting their choice of candidate.” They attributed “the confusion caused (and intended to be caused) by Daniel J. Sullivan's campaign, egged on by Peltola's” to the two campaigns.

Peltola said in a statement that voters “sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in.” “I'm eager to move forward and get to work on behalf of all Alaskans,” she said.

Her victory gives Democrats 56 seats in the coming Senate and marked their ninth Senate pickup in the midterms. Peltola, who is Yup'ik, will be the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate.

The lawsuit and its aftermath

The department sued in October at President Donald Trump’s direction, arguing that officials should not certify a Peltola win until an investigation established whether voters were confused. “I'm the one that said do it,” Trump told reporters that month.

The administration never explained how officials could examine possible voter confusion given the secrecy of ballots, The Associated Press reported. The New York Times reported several days into the lawsuit that messages and other records appeared to show Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting the second Sullivan.

On Oct. 28, Trump called the matter “voter fraud at the highest level.” He said Peltola “should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted, and so should the fake Dan Sullivan.”

Peltola has denied encouraging the candidacy, while Dan J. Sullivan has long said he ran independently. Alaska generally permits ballot stacking and the promotion of spoiler candidates. In June, before the federal case, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that Dan J. Sullivan could remain on the ballot.

Attorneys for Alaska’s Republican-controlled government opposed the federal suit as meritless and sought its dismissal. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the case, and the department appealed.

Gleason found that the government lacked standing, the Alaska Beacon reported. NPR reported that she concluded the requested order would clearly violate Alaskan voters’ right to a secret ballot.

On appeal, the League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause asked the 9th Circuit to summarily uphold the dismissal and punish the federal attorneys who filed the case. “The legal theory advanced by the United States here is embarrassing and indefensible,” American Civil Liberties Union attorneys for the groups wrote earlier.

The Beacon, citing the Anchorage Daily News, reported that the Alaska Bureau of Investigation and the FBI are investigating whether laws were broken in the second Sullivan’s recruitment.

Alaska Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher said Wednesday that she intends to certify the election, including Peltola’s win, next week.
news.summary: Mary Peltola won 50.13% of the vote, enough for an outright majority without a ranked-choice count.
news.author: Inquisitr Politics Desk

news.title: White House names Kirsten Davies new US cyber chief amid nationwide outages
news.text: The White House on Thursday named Kirsten Davies as the new U.S. national cyber director, following a series of widespread technology outages that disrupted essential services across the country and fueled public concern about the security of critical infrastructure. The appointment comes as President Donald Trump faces mounting criticism over the administration's handling of the disruptions. Davies, currently chief information officer at the Defense Department, will replace Sean Cairncross as the administration's top cybersecurity official. Several members of Trump's Cabinet announced the appointment in social media posts. "Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," Davies wrote on X. "Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future." The appointment follows a turbulent week in which a succession of major technology failures disrupted daily life for millions of Americans. Outages affected Microsoft services, Chase Bank, air traffic control systems and the National Security Agency, causing flight delays, interrupting work, restricting access to banking services and disrupting classified communications. The cascade of failures prompted criticism of the Trump administration, including from some of the president's staunchest supporters. Several allies accused officials of misleading Americans or withholding information about the underlying causes of the outages, fueling uncertainty over whether the incidents were connected. Secretary of State Marco Rubio sought to calm concerns Tuesday, saying there was "zero" information indicating that the technical failures were linked to one another or caused by a malicious actor. His remarks came as speculation continued over the unusual succession of disruptions affecting major public and private systems. Trump, who returned from a three-day trip to Asia as the administration announced the appointment, played down the outages. Addressing the disruptions, the president said that "things like that happen." Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth welcomed Davies' appointment, praising her experience and commitment to the administration's priorities. "She has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump's America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape," Hegseth wrote on X.
news.summary: Kirsten Davies replaces Sean Cairncross after disruptions hit banks, airlines, Microsoft services and classified communications; even Trump allies demand answers, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio says there is no evidence the failures are connected or caused by malicious actors

news.title: Trump Administration Seeks to Drop Lawsuit in High-Stakes Alaska Senate Race
news.text:
The Trump administration on Thursday moved to abandon its lawsuit challenging the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola’s victory in Alaska’s US Senate race, ending a widely criticized effort by President Donald Trump to keep one of his political opponents from taking office.

The dispute focused on the ballot listing of a second candidate who shared the name of incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court had already ruled that the second Sullivan was legally entitled to run and remain on the ballot.

Attorneys for Alaska, whose government is controlled by Republicans, also opposed the administration’s action. They described the lawsuit as legally “meritless” and filed documents supporting its dismissal. The administration asked an appeals court Thursday to declare the case moot, two days after the election was resolved.

In its filing, Justice Department attorneys asked the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals to reverse the lower court’s dismissal, effectively erase the loss, and then dismiss the case on procedural grounds. The department said the court “should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground.”

The move came after Peltola secured an outright majority in the contest, becoming Democrats’ 56th senator and delivering the party its ninth Senate pickup in a midterm rout. She received more votes than the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan.

Requests for comment were sent to the campaigns of Peltola and Sen. Sullivan, as well as the Alaska Department of Law.

SEE ALSO: San Diego Transit Worker Dies After 12,000-Volt Electrical Exposure

The Justice Department filed the lawsuit at Trump’s direction, arguing that Peltola’s victory should not be certified until an investigation determined whether voters had been confused by the candidates’ similar names. The administration did not explain how such an investigation could be conducted given the secrecy of the ballot.

The lawsuit was filed before The New York Times published texts and other documents that appeared to indicate Peltola’s campaign had helped recruit a retired schoolteacher from the small fishing community of Petersburg. He appeared on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation, while the senator was identified as a Republican and the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan has consistently said he entered the race independently, and Peltola has denied any involvement.

Trump also called for Peltola to be prosecuted over the alleged scheme, while federal investigators descended on Alaska before Election Day. Decoy-candidate tactics like the second Sullivan’s campaign have been used in American politics for decades, including by Trump’s allies, although such efforts have occasionally resulted in criminal charges.

It was the second time since the Nov. 3 election that the Justice Department had moved to withdraw a high-profile lawsuit involving a state’s administration of its elections.

Days after Democrats took control of Congress and won major victories in gubernatorial and state legislative contests, the Justice Department moved to drop a separate lawsuit aimed at stopping California officials from counting about 20,000 ballots. The Trump administration claimed the ballots were cast by suspected noncitizens, but election officials challenged the reliability of the data and said the government’s list included many US citizens.

news.title: Trump bought up to $265,000 of Nvidia stock in September, disclosure shows
news.text:
US President Donald Trump bought up to $265,000 in Nvidia stock and sold up to $15,000 worth of the stock in September, weeks before reports surfaced about CEO Jensen Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy, according to Trump's latest financial disclosure released Thursday.

US lawmakers have asked questions about Trump's knowledge of Huang's personal life, and the president has said he "was amazed" by the allegations against Huang, one of the president's closest Silicon Valley allies.

Trump administration officials are ​currently weighing policies that could shape Nvidia's future, including rules governing exports of its advanced chips. Nvidia faces heightened scrutiny after ​news reports surfaced that Huang had a romantic relationship with a woman accused of spying for Beijing. Reuters ⁠has not independently confirmed that the woman is a spy.

The Nvidia trades were among hundreds the president made in September, according to the disclosure Trump signed on November 1 and the US Office of Government Ethics made public on Thursday. In August, Trump bought ​as much as $1.6 million worth of Nvidia shares and sold as much as $1 million worth, Reuters previously reported.

Trump also bought as much as $315,000 in SpaceX stock in September, according to the same disclosure. SpaceX is a US military contractor run by Trump's former adviser Elon Musk. 

The company has billions of dollars' ​worth of contracts with the US government, and its fortunes are often tied to approvals from federal agencies. Trump has traded SpaceX stock ​during his second term as president, including in June and July 2026.

Reuters could not immediately determine the precise amount of Trump's trades because federal officials use ranges to declare asset values on their financial disclosure forms.

TRUMP'S PORTFOLIO MANAGED SEPARATELY: WHITE HOUSE

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement that third-party financial institutions independently manage the president's portfolio and replicate "recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000."

"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments ​are bought or sold," Ingle said.

Nvidia ​is the world's leading maker ⁠of advanced AI chips, widely used to develop cutting-edge AI systems. The US has for years sought to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, driven by concerns that China could use them ​to build weapons or superior AI tools.

Nvidia executives, including Huang, have argued for broader access to ​China. Chinese companies and ⁠researchers have also repeatedly found ways around the US export restrictions.

On Monday, the Trump administration said it would further limit China’s access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia by restricting shipments of advanced chips to Southeast Asian countries, which Chinese companies have used to access computing power ⁠to train ​AI models.

The New York Times reported that Trump had been briefed in 2025 ​on Huang's relationship with the woman and on intelligence that she was giving information to the Chinese government, and that he chose not to act on the findings. Questioned ​about the New York Times reporting, Trump said he "was amazed" by the allegations against Huang.
